abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)-an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. By optimizing aptamers targeting the Zα domain of ADAR1 p150 and embedding them in a circular RNA scaffold, MARRS enables near-complete adenosine-to-inosine editing of RNA targets in cultured cells and mouse models, achieving efficiencies up to 100% in vitro and 84% in vivo. MARRS also exhibits remarkable versatility across a range of transcript targets while maintaining high specificity with minimal off-target effects. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform.

abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

abstract: The bacterium Rhodococcus equi is a common cause of severe pneumonia in foals worldwide. Foals are exposed to R. equi from birth and are most susceptible in the first weeks of life. In North America, control measures are limited to transfusion to newborn foals of hyperimmune plasma whose potency is assessed by surpassing a threshold of IgG against the virulence-associated protein A (VapA) of R. equi. Here we report results of vaccination of pregnant mares with mRNA encoding a GPI-anchored virulence-associated protein A (VapA) of R. equi induced VapA-specific IgG subisotypes transferred to their foals during the 63-day period after birth. Pregnant mares were randomly assigned to receive either VapA mRNA vaccine (n=10) at 8 and 10 months of gestation or no vaccine (n=10). Serum was collected from mares at 8 months of gestation (before vaccination for immunized mares) and {approx}24 hours after foaling and from foals at ages 1, 35, and 63 days. Mean relative concentrations of were low before immunization in all mares and did not change over time in unvaccinated mares; however, mean relative concentrations of anti-VapA IgG1, IgG4/7, and IgG3/5 of mares were significantly increased after VapA mRNA immunization and strongly correlated with the corresponding concentrations in their foals sera at age {approx}24 hours. Concentrations of anti-VapA IgGs remained increased in foals of vaccinated mares compared with control foals for at least 35 days.

abstract: The goal of this clinical trial is to test if the drug SKY-0515, an oral medication, can lower harmful proteins linked to Huntington's Disease (HD) and improve the symptoms of participants with HD. This study includes men and women aged 25 and older who have HD confirmed by genetic testing and meet certain requirements for physical ability and independence.
description: This study is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted across multiple sites. This clinical trial aims to evaluate the safety, pharmacodynamics, and efficacy of SKY-0515, a novel, orally administered small molecule. Huntington's Disease (HD) is a rare, inherited neurodegenerative condition caused by a mutation in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, resulting in excessive production of mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein, which damages nerve cells and leads to progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. SKY-0515 is designed to reduce mHTT protein levels, leading to a decrease in both wild-type and mutant forms of HTT protein. Additionally, the drug lowers postmeiotic segregation 1 (PMS1) protein, which plays a role in somatic CAG repeat expansion-a key driver of HD progression. Participants must be aged 25 or older, have genetically confirmed HD (CAG repeat length ≥ 40), and meet specific functional and motor criteria. They will be assigned randomly to one of four treatment arms (three doses of SKY-0515 and one placebo group). Safety and efficacy will be evaluated through blood tests, imaging (MRI), and clinical assessments, including the Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale (UHDRS).

outcomes.description: cUHDRS includes the Total Functional Capacity (range, 0-13; higher score means better functioning), Total Motor Score (range, 0-124; higher score means worse motor severity), Symbol Digit Modality Test (range, 0-110, correctly paired numbers-symbols in 90 seconds; higher score means better cognitive performance), and Stroop Color and Word Test (range, 0-no max value, correctly read color words in 45 seconds; higher score means better cognitive performance) scores. A z-score for each test is calculated, which alone can be used to describe relationship between an individual's test score and the mean score of a target population. A z-score of 0 is the mean, and ±1 is 1 standard deviation from the mean. For cUHDRS, z-scores of each test are summed, whereby a higher cUHDRS score is better (score of -3.06-no max value) and a change of ≥1.2 is a meaningful worsening, shown to track functional decline.
outcomes.measure: Change From Baseline in the Z-score from the Composite Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale (cUHDRS)

outcomes.description: The total motor score (TMS) assessed motor features of HD with standardized ratings of oculomotor function, dysarthria, chorea, dystonia, gait, and postural stability. Some items (such as chorea and dystonia) required grading each extremity (face, bucco-oral-lingual, and trunk) separately. Eye movements require both horizontal and vertical grades. The total motor impairment score is the sum of all the individual 31 motor sub-items (each rated from 0 to 4), with higher scores indicating more severe motor impairment than lower scores. The range of TMS is 0-124.
outcomes.measure: Change from Baseline in Total Motor Score (TMS)

outcomes.description: TFC consists of five ordinally scaled items assessing a person's capacity with: (1) occupation; (2) financial affairs; (3) domestic responsibilities; (4) activities of daily living; and (5) independent living. Total score ranges from zero (worst) to 13 (best).

abstract: This study will evaluate 2 dose levels of mRNA-1283 in participants ≥6 months to \<12 years to determine the optimal dose level per age group.
description:
mRNA-1283 will be administered at 2 different dose levels (Dose Level 1 and Dose Level 2), with mRNA-1273 serving as the active comparator. Dose Level 1 will be the lower dose, and Dose Level 2 will be the higher dose.

The study will consist of 2 cohorts. In Cohort 1, mRNA-1283 will be administered as a single dose to participants aged ≥2 to \<12 years, regardless of prior coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccination status, with mRNA-1273 included as a comparator. In Cohort 2, mRNA-1283 will be administered as a 2-dose series to participants aged ≥6 months to \<2 years who are previously unvaccinated for COVID-19, with mRNA-1273 included as a comparator.

abstract:
Background:

CGD is caused by a gene mutation. For people with CGD, their cells cannot kill germs well, so they can get frequent or life-threatening infections. Researchers want to see if a new procedure can help a person s cells kill germs for a short time. It uses messenger RNA (mRNA) to deliver correct instructions for the gene mutation to the cells.

Objective:

To test a procedure in which mRNA is added to a person s blood cells.

Eligibility:

Males aged 18-75 with CGD with a mutation in the gene that makes the protein gp91phox.

Design:

Participants will be screened with:

Medical history

Physical exam

Blood and urine tests

Swab to test for strep throat

Some screening tests will be repeated during the study.

Participants will be admitted to the NIH Clinical Center hospital for at least 7 days. They will have apheresis. For this, a medicine is injected under their skin to prepare their white blood cells for collection. An IV line is placed into an arm vein. Blood goes through the IV line into a machine that divides whole blood into red blood cells, plasma, and white blood cells. The white blood cells are removed, and the rest of the blood is returned to the participant through an IV line in their other arm. The next day, they will get their mRNA-corrected cells via IV. They will be monitored for 3 more days.

After discharge, participants will keep a symptom diary. They will be contacted weekly for one month, and then once a month. They will have a follow-up visit 3 months after the infusion....

description:
Study Design:

This is a phase 1, open-label, dose-escalation trial to assess the safety and feasibility of administering CGD-Grans to adult patients with X-linked CGD and to identify the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Subjects will undergo granulocyte-enriched apheresis to provide cell product for mRNA-correction and then receive 1 administration of study agent. The first subjects enrolled will receive the study agent at the lowest dose, and when a level has been determined to be safe, the dose level will be increased to a second and then third dose level for subsequent subjects.Subjects will be hospitalized for at least 3 days after study agent administration and will return for a final study visit about 3 months after administration. Blood will be collected regularly for safety and research evaluations. The study hypothesis is that it is safe and feasible to administer mRNA-transfected autologous granulocyte-enriched apheresis product to restore protein expression and phagocyte nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase function in patients with CGD.

Study Agent Description:

The study agent is one administration of autologous CGD mRNA transfected granulocyte-enriched cells, referred to as CGD-Grans. The study agent is derived from apheresis product enriched for granulocytes, which are then transfected with CGD mRNA and administered as an intravenous (IV) infusion. CGD-Grans will be evaluated using the 3+3 modified Fibonacci model at the following 3 escalating dosages:

Dose K: 1 x 10\^6 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Dose K+1: 1 x 10\^7 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Dose K+2: 1-5 x 10\^8 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Each dose will be evaluated in at least 3 subjects. Dose escalation will be managed by a predetermined algorithm depending on the occurrence of drug-related toxicity (DRT). There will be at least 1 week between study agent administration to each subject.

Primary Objectives:

1. Determine the safety and feasibility of CGD-Grans infusion.
2. Determine an MTD for administration.

Secondary Objectives:

1. Assess efficacy of CGD-Grans at restoring NADPH oxidase.
2. Determine the kinetics of CGD-Grans.

Exploratory Objectives:

1. Assess for inflammatory responses to CGD-Grans infusion.
2. Assess for immune responses to protein expressed by the transfected mRNA.
3. Evaluate in vitro bactericidal activity of CGD-Grans.

Primary Endpoints:

1. Determine safety and feasibility by:

   Safety: Frequency of grade 3 or greater adverse events (AEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs) related to the study agent.

   Feasibility: Recruitment, implementation, and manufacturing of CGD-Grans for infusions.
2. MTD determination based on the rate of AEs. MTD is defined as the highest dose level that does not cause the same grade 3 or 4 AEs in 3 or more patients.

Secondary Endpoints:

1. Determine percent of circulating dihydrorhodamine (DHR) positive granulocytes following study agent infusion.
2. Serial measurement of circulating DHR+ granulocytes from peripheral blood until day 3 following study agent infusion or disappearance of DHR+ granulocytes.

Exploratory Endpoint:

1. Assess for increased expression of inflammation-related genes after study agent infusion.
2. Evaluate for development of antibodies against mRNA-expressed CGDphox.
3. Perform in vitro bactericidal activity of CGD-Grans.

abstract: The goal of this study is to determine the safety and antitumor effects of REM-422, a MYB mRNA degrader, in people with Higher Risk MDS and relapsed/refractory AML
description:
This is a Phase 1, open-label, non-randomized, multicenter study investigating REM-422, a potent, selective, and oral small molecule mRNA degrader that reduces expression of the MYB transcription factor for patients with higher risk MDS or relapsed/refractory AML.

This study includes a Dose Escalation Phase and a Dose Expansion Phase. The purpose of the Dose Escalation Phase is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and/or recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D) of REM-422 in patients with higher risk MDS or relapsed/refractory AML. The purpose of Dose Expansion is to further evaluate the safety and anti-tumor activity of the RP2D carried forward from Dose Escalation.

Participation in this study will continue until disease progression, therapy intolerance, or participant withdrawal.

description:
This study is an open-label, two-arm, multi-step phase I study evaluating a combination of two broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs), VRC07-523LS and PGT121.414.LS, in people living with HIV (PWH) who started antiretroviral therapy (ART) during acute/early infection. Participants will receive PGT121.414.LS and VRC07-523LS prior to undergoing an analytical treatment interruption (ATI). Participants will restart ART and continue follow-up after ATI to confirm viral suppression.

Participants will be screened for eligibility and have a pre-entry visit. After determination of eligibility, participants will be enrolled sequentially into Arm A (n=20) and then Arm B (n=20). The study consists of three steps including an analytic treatment interruption.

Arm A:

* Step 1: Participants remain on ART and will receive an infusion of VRC07-523LS and PGT121.414.LS at study entry.
* Step 2: Participants will interrupt their ART and receive a second infusion of VRC07-523LS 12 weeks after the initial infusion. Participants will be monitored closely for indications to resume ART.
* Step 3: Upon meeting ART restart criteria in Step 2; participants will resume ART and be followed for up to 24 weeks.

Arm B:

* Step 1: Participants remain on ART and will receive an infusion of VRC07-523LS and PGT121.414.LS at study entry and a second infusion of VRC07-523LS 12 weeks later.
* Step 2: Participants will interrupt their ART. Participants will be monitored closely for indications to resume ART.
* Step 3: Upon meeting ART restart criteria in Step 2; participants will resume ART and be followed for up to 24 weeks.

Participation in both arms will last up to 98 weeks.

abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus has recently emerged in dairy cattle in the USA, leading to mastitis and sharp reductions in milk production. The main site of H5N1 viral replication is the mammary tissue rather than the respiratory tract and viral transmission between animals is thought to occur through viral shedding in milk. Here, we generate an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccine encoding the hemagglutinin (HA) of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, representative of circulating bovine H5N1 viruses, and assess its immunogenicity and efficacy in lactating dairy cows. Eight cows were divided into vaccinated and control groups, receiving two intramuscular doses of the vaccine or saline, followed by intramammary viral challenge. Vaccination elicited HA-reactive and neutralizing antibodies in serum and HA-reactive antibodies in milk. Following viral challenge, vaccinated cows had ~1,000-fold lower peak viral RNA in milk and a lower occurrence of mastitis and mammary fibrosis.

title: An mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine against H5N1 influenza virus protects lactating dairy cows from infection.

abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3-5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy-lysosome pathway constitute the core proteolytic metabolic networks that maintain cellular protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and organelle metabolic identity. Intracellular pathogens frequently reprogram host metabolic pathways to establish replicative niches, yet how they manipulate proteostatic metabolism to remodel organelle maturation remains incompletely understood.
METHODS: CelF secretion was confirmed by TEM translocation assay. CRISPR-dCas9 was used to generate CelF knockdown and complementation strains, with celF transcription verified by RT-qPCR. Cell infection and SCID mouse models were used to assess intracellular survival, Coxiella-containing vacuole (CCV) maturation, and virulence of Coxiella burnetii. The effect of CelF on late autophagy was examined by dual-fluorescence LC3 and Western blotting. Then, UBQLN1 was identified as a CelF-interacting host protein by co-IP and pull-down, followed by truncation mapping. Finally, co-IP, UBQLN1 knockdown, Western blotting and MST assays were used to analyze the effect of CelF on SNARE assembly, SNAP29 degradation and ubiquitination, and competitive binding of CelF and PSMD4 to UBQLN1.
RESULTS: CelF depletion severely impaired the metabolic maturation of CCV, suppressed bacterial proliferation in macrophages, and attenuated virulence in vivo. Mechanistically, CelF acted as a molecular decoy that directly bound the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain of the proteasomal shuttle factor UBQLN1, competitively displacing the proteasome subunit PSMD4. This competitive interference blocked UBQLN1-mediated proteasomal delivery of SNAP29 without altering its ubiquitination status, thereby enhancing SNAP29 protein stability and promoting assembly of the STX17-SNAP29-VAMP8 fusogenic complex. The augmented SNARE activity drove autophagosome-lysosome fusion, sustained autophagic flux, and facilitated lysosomal metabolic remodeling to support CCV biogenesis.
DISCUSSION: Unlike canonical pathogen-encoded UPS modulators that function as E3 ligases or deubiquitinases, CelF operates purely through competitive protein-protein interaction, representing a previously unrecognized paradigm for microbial manipulation of host proteostatic metabolism. Our findings reveal that intracellular pathogens can actively orchestrate organelle metabolic identity by rewiring host proteostasis, and identify the UBQLN1-PSMD4-SNAP29 axis as a novel regulatory checkpoint for SNARE proteostasis and lysosomal metabolic maturation.

title: Coxiella burnetii effector CelF reprograms host proteostasis via competitive disruption of the UBQLN1-PSMD4 axis to stabilize autophagic SNARE SNAP29 and modulate lysosomal metabolic maturation.

abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. The median survival time after diagnosis is 2 to 5 years. Oxidative stress (OS), driven mainly by reactive oxygen species (ROS), plays a central role in motor neuron (MN) degeneration. In this narrative review, we analyse the pathogenic role of SOD1 variants and their contribution to OS in ALS. SOD1 mutations alter the Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative damage and triggering neuroinflammatory cascades via the MAPK, NF-κB and Nrf2/ARE signalling pathways. We also discuss emerging proteomic and machine-learning biomarkers, as well as the current therapeutic landscape. Riluzole and edaravone are approved treatments, while AMX0035 was approved in 2022 but withdrawn in 2024. Masitinib and EPI-589 remain investigational. In the realm of genetic therapies, the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for SOD1-ALS, primarily due to its ability to reduce plasma neurofilament light chain levels. However, the clinical benefit remains modest. RNA interference has reached human trials, while CRISPR/Cas9 remains in the preclinical stage. Both approaches have shown promising results in experimental models. Further research into ALS pathogenesis is needed to develop treatments that integrate antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gene-editing strategies.

outcomes.description: Fatigue will be assessed with the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue subscale (FACIT-F). The FACIT-F Scale is a 13-item scale used to measure self-reported fatigue. Items are assessed on a 5-point Likert scale, with responses ranging from 0 for "not at all" to 4 for "very much". outcomes.description: The RAND KDQOL-36 is an abbreviated questionnaire that combines the generic and disease-specific components to assess participant's health-related quality of life. This 36-item questionnaire includes the RAND 12, Version 1 (12 items) and 3 disease-related domains, symptoms/problems (12 items), burden of kidney disease (4 items), and effects of kidney disease (8 items). It uses a recall of 4 weeks, and items are assessed on 3- to 5-point Likert scales or with a dichotomous response option. Higher score indicates better health. The raw scores are transformed linearly to a range of 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better health.

abstract: Chronic lung diseases arise from complex interactions between environmental exposures and host genetic factors. However, these interactions are not fully understood, and despite decades of study, effective curative therapies remain unavailable for many patients. Recent breakthroughs in therapeutic gene-editing have become a reality for some inherited blood diseases and are a promising approach for monogenic lung diseases. Early-phase clinical studies are now ongoing for AATD, primarily through liver-directed editing of hepatocytes to restore circulating functional AAT and for COVID-19 using gene-edited immune cell approaches. However, direct in vivo gene-editing of pulmonary epithelial cells remains largely at the preclinical stage. Expanding this therapeutic pipeline requires overcoming the unique biological barriers of the lung and developing human-specific models that faithfully recapitulate human disease mechanisms. Advances in gene-editing technologies, including CRISPR-Cas9 systems, base and prime editors, and emerging compact nucleases, have increased the feasibility of precise genomic correction. However, safe and efficient delivery directly to the lung remains a major unmet challenge due to mucus, surfactant, epithelial tight junctions, and innate immune surveillance. Delivery systems such as engineered AAVs, lentiviral vectors, selective organ targeting lipid nanoparticles and aerosolizable formulations like nebulised or dry powder nanoparticles are beginning to address these obstacles. In parallel, human preclinical models have evolved from traditional cell lines to more sophisticated platforms such as iPSC-derived airway and alveolar cells, organoids, precision-cut lung slices, air-liquid interface cultures, organ-on-a-chip devices, and patient-derived primary cells. These models enable mechanistic interrogation, variant-specific functional assessment, and preclinical evaluation of gene-editing strategies with increased physiological relevance. In this review, we detail current and emerging gene-editing tools, delivery strategies, and human-relevant disease models. We highlight key translational barriers and discuss how advanced human models combined with improved delivery technologies can accelerate the development of safe and effective gene-editing therapeutics for chronic respiratory disease.

title: Gene-Editing in Respiratory Disease: From Pre-Clinical Human Models to Future Therapeutics.

abstract: Background/Objectives: CRISPR/Cas-dependent base editing enables the precise correction of genomic sequences by direct modification of DNA bases without creating potentially mutagenic DNA double-strand breaks. Base editing is considered a therapeutic approach for rare monogenic disorders or viral infections. However, many variants of base editors suffer from limited specificity because they induce bystander edits within a broad editing window. However, nucleotide substitution is sufficient to correct a mutation or to achieve a therapeutic effect. Methods: PCR, cloning by restriction digest, and ligation were used to create genetic constructs. The editing efficiency was evaluated using NGS. Virus-like particles were produced in HEK293T cells using transient expression. VLPs were visualized by electron microscopy. Results: Using dual base editors that induce C-to-T and A-to-G substitutions, we show that high editing precision can be achieved by engineering the linker between the MmCas12m domain and the deaminase domain of the editor. By testing different linker sequences, we have created high-precision dual base editors with narrowed editing windows that can edit a single nucleotide at a target position with high accuracy. Conclusions: We found that shortening the linker to an acceptable length provides a single-nucleotide substitution in vitro with minimal bystander activity (less than 0.8%), while the high-precision MmCas12m dual base editor retains up to 90% of the editing efficiency of the original base editor. These high-precision base editors will be useful in cases where high precision is required, and editing of adjacent nucleotides is undesirable.

abstract: Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy, its efficacy against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains severely limited, highlighting an urgent need for novel targets and strategies to overcome immune evasion. Here, we aimed to identify key regulators of HCC immunity via unbiased functional screening and develop a targeted therapy to remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed an in vivo CRISPR-knockout screen using a 4500-gene sgRNA library in syngeneic HCC mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing of human HCC tissues and in vivo macrophage-depletion assays were utilized to dissect cellular populations and validate underlying mechanisms. We identified ribosomal protein S19 (RPS19) as a central mediator of HCC immune evasion, whose deletion in HCC cells mitigates the immunosuppressive TME. Mechanistically, scRNA-seq pinpointed tumor-associated macrophages as the key effector subset, whereby complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) transduces RPS19 signals to trigger macrophage-dependent immune suppression. We further constructed SP94-peptide-modified disulfide-bond-containing nanoparticles (SNPSS) for targeted CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. SNPSS efficiently homes to HCC cells, releases payloads within the glutathione-rich TME, downregulates RPS19, reverses immune suppression, and robustly suppresses HCC progression in vivo. Collectively, the RPS19-C5aR1-macrophage axis fuels HCC immune escape, and SNPSS-based RPS19 gene-editing offers a promising strategy to remodel the TME and boost HCC immunotherapy efficacy.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Screen Identifies RPS19 as an Immunotherapy Target in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.

abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)-SE regulating IL1A, IL1B, and IL36G transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE-centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

title: FOSL1-associated condensates modulate superenhancer-mediated selected IL-1 family gene activation in psoriasis.

abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is still a global health challenge, as there is no effective treatment due to the inadequacy of conventional experimental platforms for comprehending pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapy. Objectives: This review details the recent progress and clinical utility of next-generation iPSC-derived 3D in vitro systems integrated with microfluidics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, multi-omics readouts, and AI-based machine learning, which are emerging as transformative platforms for recapitulating key ALS pathological hallmarks. Methods: A literature search was performed using PubMed and Web of Science, including only English-language publications. All the published papers collected covered the period from January 2015 to June 2026. Results: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cerebral organoids, assembloids, and organ-on-a-chip technologies are revolutionizing research into ALS by providing a way to model the complex spatial organization, cellular heterogeneity, and neural network dynamics of the human brain. Moreover, recent bioengineering advancements enable the inclusion of functional neurovascular units, the integration of resident immune cells (microglia), and the use of 3D bioprinting to accelerate the functional maturation of age-related phenotypes. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, OMICS, and machine learning improve tools for studying ALS and identifying therapeutic targets. Conclusions: Novel cell culture models may bridge the gap between preclinical animal models and human clinical trials and reduce the duration and costs of translation. Future work is likely to integrate bioprinting with organ-on-chip microfluidics, CRISPR-based genetic editing, and multi-omics readouts to build increasingly faithful, patient-specific ALS models for both basic research and precision therapeutics.

title: Advancing the Translational Pipeline: From In Vivo and In Vitro 2D Models to Next-Generation Cell Culture Models for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Modelling and Drug Discovery.

abstract:
AIM: In vitro air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures of human airway epithelial cells are widely used to study respiratory biology and disease, as they recapitulate key features of the pseudostratified airway epithelium and reduce reliance on animal models and repeated patient biopsies. However, the limited proliferative capacity of primary airway basal cells restricts long-term studies and genome editing. This study aimed to generate stable, immortalised human airway basal cell lines that retain differentiation capacity and support genetic manipulation.
METHODS: Human airway epithelial basal cells from bronchial and nasal origin were immortalised by lentiviral expression of human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) followed by polyclonal expansion. A panel of cell lines derived from three independent nasal donors was established. Differentiation capacity was assessed in ALI cultures and compared with primary airway epithelial cells. Suitability for genetic manipulation was evaluated using lentiviral overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout and knock-in strategies.
RESULTS: All immortalised cell lines displayed sustained proliferative capacity and efficiently differentiated into major airway epithelial cell types, including multiciliated and secretory cells. Differentiation patterns and functional characteristics closely resembled those of primary airway epithelial cultures. The cell lines supported efficient lentiviral transduction and CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, enabling stable gene overexpression, targeted gene disruption, and precise genomic modification.
CONCLUSIONS: hTERT-immortalised human airway basal cell lines preserve key features of primary airway epithelium while enabling long-term culture and versatile genome editing. This resource provides a robust platform for airway biology research, disease modelling, and therapeutic development.

title: Immortalisation of human airway epithelial cells for genome editing applications.

abstract: CRISPR/Cas9 enables precision gene editing via homology-directed repair (HDR) for mutation correction and disease modelling. Here we present a customizable T cell single nucleotide variant (SNV) correction platform based on non-viral HDR, previously described in Mamia et al. Precision T Cell Correction Platform for Inborn Errors of Immunity. Molecular Therapy, 2025. To enable reproducible application, we provide a comprehensive, step-by-step 8-day HDR workflow for editing primary T cells, covering CRISPR/Cas9 reagent design, custom genomic editing from start to finish, optimization and validation strategies, on-target detection, and flow cytometric assessment of T cell phenotype and exhaustion. The platform separates locus-specific reagent optimization from a fixed cellular workflow, enabling implementation of new genomic targets without modifying the downstream T cell editing pipeline. Using this workflow, we have achieved up to 80% editing efficiency across multiple loci and donors. We have further optimized the T cell culture platform for PBMC stimulation to promote CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation and proliferation. We validated this culture platform in 33 patients with Inborn Errors of Immunity using flow cytometry and observed that the defined culture conditions maintain low T cell exhaustion and support persistence of memory T cell populations. The protocol was developed under research-grade conditions but supports scalability and transition to preclinical and clinical GMP workflows. Overall, this adaptable platform is a broadly applicable framework for precision T cell engineering across diverse genomic targets offering opportunities for both in vitro disease modeling and therapeutic genome correction.

title: Protocol for non-viral HDR-based CRISPR/Cas9 platform for small custom editing in primary T cells.

abstract: A GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of C9orf72 is the most common monogenic cause of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD). This element serves as a template for repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation, which generates neurotoxic dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins that aggregate in patient brains and contribute to neurodegeneration in model systems. To understand the mechanisms underlying RAN translation initiation, we used cryo-electron microscopy to determine the structure of an in vitro assembled human late-stage C9orf72 translation initiation complex at 3.2 A resolution and a near-native complex purified from human cell lysate at 3.5 A resolution. RAN translation on C9orf72 mRNA initiates predominantly at a near-cognate CUG codon that is located 24 nucleotides upstream of the G4C2 repeat and is flanked by a strong endogenous Kozak sequence. The structures further reveal a direct interaction between the G4C2 repeat and 18S ribosomal RNA expansion segment 9 (ES9S) on the 40S small ribosomal subunit through a kissing-loop interaction. Preventing this RNA-RNA interaction using complementary antisense oligonucleotides significantly reduces RAN translation in vitro and in patient-derived iNeurons, indicating that this structural interaction is functionally important. These findings provide mechanistic insights into RAN translation initiation and highlight a novel potential therapeutic approach to mitigate toxic DPR production in C9orf72-associated neurodegenerative disease.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered natural killer (NK) cell therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer treatment, offering advantages over CAR-T cells such as a lower risk of cytokine release syndrome and graft-versus-host disease and the potential for off-the-shelf manufacturing. Viral vectors have long served as effective tools for CAR-NK engineering, but their dependence on complex manufacturing procedures, considerable production costs, and the potential risks associated with genomic integration has encouraged increasing interest in non-viral alternatives. Recent advances in genetic engineering technologies have facilitated the development of CAR-NK platforms, particularly through non-viral delivery approaches including electroporation, transposon systems and lipid nanoparticles, while CRISPR-based tools enable targeted genome editing. Meanwhile, an increasing number of clinical trials have begun to evaluate the safety and therapeutic potential of CAR-NK cells in both hematological malignancies and solid tumors. However, challenges such as limited NK-cell persistence, antigen heterogeneity, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remain. In this review, we summarize recent progress in non-viral CAR-NK engineering strategies, analyze the current landscape of preclinical and clinical trials, and discuss key challenges and future directions for advancing CAR-NK therapy. Collectively, these advances suggest that non-viral engineering technologies may serve as an important technological foundation for next-generation CAR-NK therapies, enabling more flexible ex vivo manufacturing and potentially supporting the future development of in vivo CAR-NK generation strategies for solid tumors.

title: Non-viral delivery and genome editing for CAR-NK engineering in solid tumors: from ex vivo manufacturing to in vivo reprogramming.

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted global supply chains, causing shortages of critical lipid-based raw materials for mRNA vaccine production. To enhance formulation resilience, we systematically evaluated the impact of five ionizable lipids (ILs) on lipid nanoparticle (LNP) organization, mRNA delivery and immunogenicity. The physiochemical analysis revealed the potential coexistence of liquid crystalline lamellar (Lα) and inverse hexagonal (HII) phases, or a mixture of nucleotide-loaded and non-loaded HII phases within developed LNP formulations. Furthermore, ILs with saturated, multi-tail structures, such as Lipid-5 and SM-102, favored inverse hexagonal (HII) internal organization and fusion intermediates, correlating with enhanced endosomal fusion and higher in vivo protein expression. In contrast, ILs such as cKK-E12, which featured dual ionization headgroups and tended to form lamellar-like structures, showed reduced encapsulation efficiency and transfection potency. The preclinical experiments demonstrated that all developed formulations induced robust binding and neutralizing antibody responses; however, antibody responses were lower in mRNA Lipid 5 LNPs and mRNA SM-102 LNPs than in other formulations. Notably, within the limited panel of ILs in this study, protein expression levels did not show a clear correlation with antibody titers, highlighting that efficient antigen expression alone is not predictive of humoral immunity. These findings underscore how IL structural features influence LNP architecture and function, informing the rational design of next-generation mRNA vaccines.

title: Ionizable lipid impact on mRNA vaccine formulation properties and immunogenicity.

abstract: Delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) using synthetic materials can bypass the host translational machinery and limit the duration of genomic exposure, minimizing the risk of off-target mutations. Despite their advantages, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platforms for CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery that achieve highly efficient editing at low doses remain limited. In the present study, we developed a library of ionizable lipids (ILs) and corresponding LNPs to enhance the delivery and editing efficiencies of CRISPR-Cas9 RNP complexes. Following comprehensive in vitro screening and formulation optimization, an optimal LNP candidate containing the C12A9 IL (denoted as LNPC12A9) was identified that achieved ∼90% EGFP disruption in HEK293T-EGFP cells at an RNP concentration of 30 nM and ∼60% at 15 nM. The editing performance was consistently observed at an RNP concentration of 15 nM when editing the Gcgr and HPRT1 genes across multiple hepatic cell lines. Moreover, coencapsulation of RNP and a single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) template for homology-directed repair (HDR) within LNPC12A9 induced an HDR rate of 37.8%. Systemic administration of LNPC12A9 into C57BL/6J mice led to liver tropism and a total hepatic Pcsk9 gene disruption rate of 1.39%. In conclusion, this study provides insights into the construction of an LNP platform to improve the delivery efficiency of CRISPR-Cas9 RNP, thereby facilitating the development of LNPs for safe, precise, and tissue-specific Cas9 RNP-based genome editing therapies.

title: High-Throughput Screening of a Lipid Nanoparticle (LNP) Library Identifies Lead Formulations for CRISPR-Cas9 Ribonucleoprotein Delivery and Gene Editing.

abstract: Chemical modifications of RNA bases and adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing are regulatory layers essentially unexplored in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), whose oxidative dysfunction underlies age-related macular degeneration. We mapped both layers in ARPE-19 cells exposed to tert-butyl hydroperoxide under two non-pharmacological interventions, Quantum Molecular Resonance (QMR) electrotherapy and a patient blood-derived secretome, across 56 libraries spanning four arms, three time points and matched stressed and stress-free conditions (GEO: GSE328981). Base modifications were called with HARMLNC and A-to-I editing screened with a transition-signal caller, then re-analysed with REDItools3, JACUSA2 and LoDEI. The high-confidence set comprised 241 calls at 15 sites, all of classes canonical to tRNA and rRNA. The most prevalent was an adenosine modification at chrM:2617 in mitochondrial 16S rRNA (MT-RNR2), detected in 51 of 56 libraries and in every arm. Two positions 1 bp apart lie in an EZR/SYTL3 overlap region, whereas a third chromosome 6 site maps to HLA-C, 127.5 Mb away. No position of either layer differed between treatment arms: 7 testable modification sites (minimum p = 0.19) and, at single-nucleotide resolution under dedicated callers agreeing to r = 0.975-0.992, 15 curated editing positions (minimum q = 0.169). Two one-sided tests bound any change in substitution composition within 1.4% and in mean editing frequency within 10% for secretome and combination and 20% for QMR. Against a stress-free baseline internal to the cohort, only chrM:13710 (MT-ND5) changed detectably (q = 0.03). These layers are therefore small, largely constitutive and quantifiably undisturbed by either intervention at the resolution available.

title: RNA base-modification and A-to-I editing landscapes of oxidatively stressed human retinal pigment epithelium under Quantum Molecular Resonance electrotherapy and blood-derived secretome.

abstract: Clinical heterogeneity remains a major challenge across human diseases, where patients with similar genetic backgrounds frequently exhibit striking differences in disease progression, therapeutic response and clinical outcome. Increasing evidence indicates that these differences cannot be explained by genetic variation alone, positioning epigenetic memory as a critical non-genetic determinant of disease behavior. Epigenetic memory refers to the stable yet reversible propagation of transcriptional states through mechanisms including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, enhancer dynamics and higher-order chromatin organization. In this review, we synthesize emerging mechanistic and translational evidence demonstrating how epigenetic memory integrates environmental, metabolic, inflammatory, infectious and therapeutic cues into persistent cellular programs that drive inter-patient, intra-tumoral and temporal heterogeneity. We discuss its disease-specific manifestations across cancer, immunological, neurological, and metabolic disorders, with particular emphasis on cellular plasticity, stemness, immune evasion, drug-tolerant persister states and relapse. Furthermore, we highlight recent advances in single-cell and spatial epigenomics, liquid-biopsy-based epigenetic biomarkers, CRISPR-mediated epigenome editing and targeted chromatin therapies that collectively establish epigenetic memory as both a measurable biomarker and a therapeutically actionable vulnerability. By framing epigenetic memory as a dynamic interface between genome and environment, this review provides a unified conceptual framework for understanding disease evolution and advancing precision epigenetic medicine.

title: Epigenetic Memory in Human Diseases: Acquired Chromatin States as Targetable Drivers of Disease Evolution.

abstract: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) comprise a biologically diverse and clinically aggressive family of mature T/NK-cell neoplasms, for which outcomes remain poor in the majority of patients treated with conventional anthracycline-based frontline regimens. Contemporary classifications (WHO-HAEM5 and ICC) increasingly incorporate immunophenotypic and molecular information, underscoring that "PTCL-NOS" is not a single disease but rather a diagnostic umbrella that includes biologically distinct entities and molecular subgroups. Among these are the TBX21- and GATA3-driven PTCL-NOS subsets, the latter associated with inferior survival and a distinctive cytokine/microenvironmental program. These advances, many of which were shaped by long-standing contributions from the Bologna group, support a rational shift from empiric chemotherapy toward mechanism-based and immune-based interventions. CAR-engineered cellular therapies have revolutionized the care of B-cell malignancies, yet translation to PTCL has been delayed by lineage-specific barriers: (i) fratricide during manufacturing when targeting shared T-cell antigens (e.g., CD5, CD7), (ii) the risk of profound and prolonged T-cell aplasia (a markedly less "replaceable" toxicity than B-cell aplasia), and (iii) product contamination by malignant T-cells in autologous platforms. Recent progress in genome editing (CRISPR/Cas9 and base editing), intracellular antigen "blocking" strategies, and alternative effectors (allogeneic "universal" CAR-T, CAR-NK, and iPSC-derived platforms) has begun to address these obstacles at the manufacturing level, while their downstream clinical consequences (e.g., prolonged cytopenias, infectious risk and delayed immune reconstitution) remain incompletely resolved. Early-phase clinical trials now demonstrate clinically meaningful responses for select targets, particularly CD7, CD5, TRBC1 and CD30, for the pan-T targets. However, the strongest efficacy data remain largely derived from T-cell lymphoblastic malignancies (T-ALL/T-LBL), whereas evidence in mature PTCL remains limited and at an earlier stage, with target-specific differences in safety, immune reconstitution and relapse patterns. This review synthesizes the biological rationale for antigen selection in PTCL, the emerging clinical evidence for leading CAR targets, and the engineering strategies most likely to improve the therapeutic index. It also proposes an integrated hematology perspective on how CAR-based therapies might be positioned relative to transplant and evolving targeted agents in relapsed/refractory PTCL.

title: Targeting Peripheral T-Cell Lymphomas with Chimeric Antigen Receptor Therapy: Mechanistic Challenges, Clinical Landscape and Future Engineering Perspectives.

abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease.

abstract: H3 subtype avian influenza virus (AIV) is one of the most widely distributed and frequently detected low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (LPAIVs) in wild birds and poultry worldwide. Wild waterfowl are the natural reservoir of this virus. In recent years, driven by frequent genetic reassortment and continuous evolution, H3 subtype AIV has expanded its host range to include various mammalian species-dogs, cats, horses, seals, pigs (experimental infection), and humans. Among these, the H3N8 subtype shows the broadest cross-species transmissibility, having established sustained transmission lineages in horses and dogs, while also causing sporadic infections in seals and humans. Avian-origin H3N2 canine influenza virus has circulated stably in dog populations across Asia and North America for nearly two decades. Between 2022 and 2023, China reported three human cases of H3N8 subtype AIV infection, one of which was fatal (Guangdong, March 2023), indicating that this virus poses a potential zoonotic transmission risk. Novel triple-reassortant strains, including genotype G25 of H3N8 and H3N3, first detected in chicken flocks in late 2022, have continued to emerge. Their HA genes originate from H3 subtype viruses of wild bird or chicken origin, whereas their internal gene segments are predominantly acquired from H9N2 subtype AIV, resulting in enhanced mammalian adaptability. This review summarizes the global epidemiology of H3 subtype AIV (covering wild birds, poultry, and live poultry markets), its genetic evolution and reassortment patterns, and the molecular mechanisms underlying cross-species transmission. This review particularly highlights the regulatory roles of key amino acid mutations-such as PB2-D701N, M1-M192V, and HA-Q226L/G228S-in receptor binding preference, polymerase activity, and pathogenicity. This review also summarizes recent advances in detection techniques (multiplex RT-PCR, quantum dot-based immunochromatographic strips, RT-RAA, and CRISPR-Cas13a) and vaccine development (inactivated, adenovirus-vectored, and mRNA vaccines). Key prevention and control challenges-including covert circulation, surveillance gaps, and limited subtyping diagnostic capacity at primary laboratories-are also discussed. This review proposes that H3 subtype AIV should be recognized as a potential zoonotic threat warranting continued surveillance, although no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission has been documented to date. Better understanding of cross-species mechanisms, stronger surveillance and early warning, and evidence-based control strategies are needed to inform future risk assessment.

title: H3 Subtype Avian Influenza Virus: Ecology, Cross-Species Evolution, and Public Health Threats.

abstract: Background: Allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are increasingly used to selectively suppress transcripts containing pathogenic gain-of-function or dominant negative (GOF/DN) variants. However, most current approaches rely on patient-specific target selection of SNVs in cis with the disease-causing variant. This individualized approach may limit broader ASO applicability and could exacerbate inequities in access. Population-level selection of ASO-targetable SNVs is an alternative approach not previously explored at scale. Methods: For a curated set of >400 disease genes with putative toxic GOF/DN mechanisms, we applied a greedy algorithm to identify ASO-targetable SNVs that maximize population coverage in the 1000 Genomes Project dataset. Population coverage was evaluated across ''superpopulation'' ancestry groups and assessed in multiple diverse replication datasets. For each prioritized SNV we attempted to design allele-specific 15-mer and 20-mer ASOs meeting standard chemistry and sequence criteria. The presence of prioritized SNVs was assessed in two local cohorts with GOF/DN disorders: infants with epilepsy diagnosed by rapid short-read genome sequencing, and children with long-read genome sequencing data generated for bespoke ASO development. Results: We identified 7,927 SNVs (median 17.5 per gene) achieving a median cumulative heterozygous population coverage of 88.9% across 408 disease genes. More than two-thirds of genes (70.6%) reached [≥]80% coverage using a median of only four prioritized SNVs. Coverage was consistently high for all ''superpopulation'' ancestry groups, with median coverage proportions of [≥]85%. Prioritized SNVs generalized to independent ancestrally diverse replication datasets, achieving median coverage of 86.4% in the Human Genome Diversity Project and 90.3% in the All of Us Research Program. Many prioritized targets were compatible with established ASO design principles, enabling generation of candidate allele-specific 15-mer and 20-mer ASOs at scale for future experimental validation. The presence of prioritized targets in the rapid short-read sequencing cohort, and the overlap between prioritized targets and manually curated long-read genome sequencing targets, supports the clinical relevance of population-informed target selection. All SNV targets and candidate allele-specific ASO sequences are available at hawk-eye.research.sickkids.ca/knockdown. Conclusions: Prioritization of common SNV targets may facilitate the development of ASO therapies with broader population coverage, helping move the field beyond single-patient applications and toward more equitable opportunities for access.

title: Population-scale genome-wide prioritization of targets for allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide therapy design

abstract: In recent years, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have shown great promise as highly flexible delivery systems for cancer vaccines, which enable effective cargo delivery and allow for controlling their distribution, cell-targeting ability and immunogenicity. Innovations in ionizable lipid chemistry, biodegradable formulations, RNA engineering and LNP design resulted in improvements in RNA encapsulation, endosomal escape, delivery outside the liver, and targeting of lymphoid organs and antigen-presenting cells. All these achievements led to an expansion of strategies for developing cancer vaccines from using only mRNA to personal neoantigen vaccines, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), peptide/protein vaccines, and multi-purpose platforms that combine antigen delivery and modulation of the immune system. LNPs are also studied as tools for altering the tumor microenvironment (TME) and boosting anti-tumor immunity through local delivery of cytokines and innate immune modulators. Preliminary clinical results with personalized mRNA neoantigen vaccines show strong potential for this approach. However, inflammatory toxicity, suitability for repeated dosing, off-target delivery, difficulties with large-scale production, formulation stability, personalized production schedule and regulatory issues are still significant challenges. New biodegradable and PEG-free formulations, innovations in manufacturing and lyophilization technology, and AI-based approaches in lipid screening could help overcome some of these problems.

title: Recent Advances in Lipid Nanoparticles for Cancer Vaccines: From Antigen Delivery to Personalized Immunotherapy.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Robust non-clinical safety models are crucial to the development and evaluation of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA)-based drugs and vaccines. In this study, we leveraged cross-study data to explore whether the Göttingen minipig could serve as an alternative to the rabbit, a commonly used species in vaccine safety assessment.
METHODS: Results from two independent toxicity studies of lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding the hemagglutinin H3 antigen, administered at equivalent dose levels, were qualitatively compared. Clinical observations, local reactions, body weight, food consumption, body temperature, clinical pathology, immunogenicity, inflammatory biomarkers, and anatomical pathology endpoints were evaluated.
RESULTS: Both species exhibited expected vaccine responses, with minor differences in local reactogenicity and body temperature. The vaccine candidate was well tolerated at the injection site in both species. However, mild and transient vaccine-related effects (i.e., injection site induration and increased body temperature) were observed only in minipigs. Transient increases in neutrophil, fibrinogen, and C-reactive protein levels were observed in both species following vaccination, consistent with an inflammatory response. Microscopic findings (i.e., inflammation at the injection site and increased germinal center cellularity in the draining lymph nodes) were comparable between species and aligned with expected immune activation following vaccination.
CONCLUSIONS: This qualitative comparison provides preliminary, supportive evidence for the potential use of the minipig as an alternative to the rabbit in non-clinical safety evaluation of mRNA vaccines, with the added benefit of larger blood volume for sampling and availability of validated key inflammatory markers.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment by enabling engineered immune cells to selectively recognize and eliminate malignant targets, with CAR-T cells establishing the first major clinical success in this field. However, severe associated toxicities, logistical complexities of autologous manufacturing, and high rates of antigen-loss relapse have accelerated the development of alternative effector platforms such as CAR-NK cells. CAR-NK cells combine antigen-directed cytotoxicity with the innate antitumor functions of natural killer cells, offering a potentially safer and more readily available off-the-shelf therapeutic strategy. Nevertheless, the clinical efficacy of CAR-NK therapy is constrained by key biological and translational hurdles: brief in vivo persistence, inadequate trafficking and solid tumor infiltration, severe susceptibility to tumor microenvironment-mediated immunosuppression, and antigen escape driven by tumor heterogeneity. These biological constraints are compounded by technical bottlenecks, including cell source variability, limited large-scale expansion capacity, ex vivo functional exhaustion, and an absence of standardized manufacturing protocols. To address these multi-faceted barriers, recent advances in genome engineering, systems biology, and computational modeling provide promising routes forward. Given that prolonged exposure to immunosuppressive niches induces functional impairment, genome-editing strategies targeting inhibitory checkpoints and persistence programs are crucial; however, enhancing persistence requires stringent safeguards to mitigate toxicity risks from constitutive signaling or genomic instability. Thus, engineering next-generation CAR-NK cells necessitates balancing extended longevity, potent cytotoxicity, and safety. Multiomics approaches facilitate deeper characterization of CAR-NK functional states and tumor-immune interactions, whereas artificial intelligence-guided engineering integrates high-dimensional biological and manufacturing data to optimize receptor design, predict therapeutic performance, and accelerate translational workflows. Collectively, these innovations support a paradigm shift toward programmable CAR-NK cells that can dynamically sense, adapt, and respond to tumor evolution, driving the transition toward autonomous, highly scalable, and precisely controllable cellular immunotherapies in precision oncology.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: There is evidence for the protective effects of antibodies targeting non-structural protein 1 (NS1) of Zika virus (ZIKV); however, effective vaccines against ZIKV remain lacking.
METHODS: In this study, lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated mRNA vaccines were designed based on the envelope domain III (EDIII) and NS1 sequences of the ZIKV FSS13025 strain, while protective efficacy was evaluated in a murine model using a ZIKV isolate obtained from Zhejiang Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Zhejiang CDC).
RESULTS: The vaccines were evaluated for key quality attributes-including particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), and encapsulation efficiency-as well as immunogenicity and protective efficacy. Both monovalent vaccine components exhibited uniform particle sizes (PDI < 0.2) and high encapsulation efficiencies (≥80%) and induced high levels of antigen-specific antibodies in mice in a dose-dependent manner. The EDIII mRNA vaccine elicited moderate ZIKV-neutralizing antibody titers as measured by PRNT50, whereas the NS1 vaccine did not induce detectable neutralizing antibodies. Both bicomponent (EDIII + NS1) mRNA vaccines induced a Th1-biased cellular immune response in mouse splenocytes, with significantly greater IFN-γ production compared with either monovalent vaccine. In viral challenge experiments using 1 × 105 PFU ZIKV (Zhejiang CDC isolate, intraperitoneal), the bicomponent vaccine provided complete protection, with 100% survival across all dose groups. In contrast, the EDIII and NS1 monovalent vaccines showed partial protection: mortality was observed in the 20 μg dose groups and exceeded 50% in the 10 μg dose groups.
CONCLUSIONS: These results demonstrate that the bicomponent EDIII + NS1 mRNA vaccine combination confers superior protective efficacy compared with either component alone, consistent with a synergistic effect between humoral and cellular immune responses. This study provides a novel strategy for next-generation Zika vaccine development.

abstract: RNA 5-methylcytidine (m5C) modification plays an essential role in regulating RNA metabolism and functions in cellular processes. Tools to achieve temporal and transcript-specific m5C editing for functional studies are still limited. Furthermore, methods enabling m5C editing triggered by specific cellular signals to study m5C functions are currently lacking. Here, we present a temporally and conditionally controlled m5C writing platform engineered through integrating abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated chemically induced proximity with split-dCas13b-NSUN2/NSUN6 technology. This system enables the writing of m5C by reconstituting the split dCas13b-based m5C editing complex at the guide RNA (gRNA)-targeted RNA transcript sites under the control of the inducer ABA. The deposition of m5C is inducible, reversible and selective. The deposited m5C is biologically active and influences the stability of endogenous mRNA transcripts. Moreover, by incorporating ABA prodrugs, the m5C writing can be triggered by signals associated with distinct physiological or disease conditions (e.g., tumor microenvironment and senescence). This conditional m5C editing strategy provides a new programmable tool for studying m5C biology in a context-dependent manner and expands the repertoire of RNA modification editing technologies.

abstract: Background: Epithelial-derived carcinomas exhibit genomic instability due to genetic mutation and epigenetic dysregulation. Mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and noncoding RNA regulation may lead to tumor progression, immune evasion, and treatment resistance. Presently, gene-based and epigenetic therapies, including CRISPR systems, RNA interference, and chromatin-modifying agents, are reported to be effective in targeted cancer treatment. Objectives: This scoping review aims to map the evidence on gene-based technologies in epithelial-derived carcinomas, including therapeutic, diagnostic, prognostic, screening, and disease-modeling applications, and to identify molecular targets, translational outcomes, and gaps in the current evidence base. The review will characterize the molecular targets, gene-based approaches, cancer types, translational applications, and reported outcomes to identify evidence gaps, translational challenges, and priorities for future research. Methods: The scoping review was conducted as per PRISMA-ScR by conducting a literature search in databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering studies published between 2016 and 2026. In the inclusion criteria, all studies and reviews related to investigating gene-based, RNA-mediated, and epigenetic therapies in epithelial cancers were included. Thirty-six studies met the eligibility criteria. Results: Amongst the studies reviewed, the most common epithelial cancers reported were hepatocellular carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, lung carcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Among the epithelial-derived carcinomas identified in this review, HCC was the most frequently represented cancer; epigenetic alterations and therapies used were RNA-based therapies, CRISPR diagnostics, and epigenetic drugs. Ovarian and breast cancers targeting BRCA pathways and chromatin remodeling produced clinical translation outcomes. Lung and colorectal cancers showed moderate epigenetic involvement, often managed through combined therapeutic strategies. Pancreatic cancer therapies were limited by challenges in drug delivery despite identifiable molecular targets. Gene therapies such as CRISPR-based gene editing, RNAi/siRNA therapies, miRNA/lncRNA targeting, and HDAC inhibition were commonly reported. Conclusions: The present study indicates that the majority of epithelial-derived carcinomas can benefit from gene-based and epigenetic therapies. Though the majority of carcinomas, such as hepatocellular, have good clinical outcomes, pancreatic cancer has limited clinical translation.

title: Current Evidence on Gene-Based and Epigenetic Therapeutic, Diagnostic, and Prognostic Strategies in Epithelial-Derived Carcinomas: A Scoping Review.

abstract: Seasonal influenza and the ongoing emergence of zoonotic influenza viruses, including highly pathogenic avian influenza A (H5N1), remain substantial global public health threats, underscoring the need for rapidly adaptable vaccine platforms. This state-of-the-art review critically evaluates the clinical development of RNA-based influenza vaccines through a comprehensive assessment of ClinicalTrials.gov records and peer-reviewed literature. Candidates were examined across four domains: seasonal influenza vaccines, pre-pandemic influenza vaccines, combination respiratory vaccines, and self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) platforms. Clinical evidence indicates that mRNA influenza vaccines consistently elicit robust humoral immune responses and, in late-stage trials, have demonstrated improved relative efficacy against influenza A compared with conventional influenza vaccines. Reactogenicity is generally more frequent with mRNA vaccines, particularly with respect to transient mild-to-moderate systemic adverse events. However, serious adverse events remain uncommon and broadly comparable to those observed with licensed comparator vaccines. Pre-pandemic and multicomponent mRNA vaccine candidates similarly demonstrate strong immunogenicity, supporting the potential of RNA platforms for both seasonal vaccination and pandemic preparedness. Clinical development of saRNA influenza vaccines has progressed through early-phase trials, although publicly available clinical data remain limited. Regulatory milestones in 2026, including U.S. approval of mRNA-1010 (mFlusiva), the first approved mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccine, and European Union authorization of mRNA-1083 (mCOMBRIAX), an mRNA-based influenza-COVID-19 combination vaccine, represent important steps in the clinical transition and implementation of RNA-based influenza vaccination.

title: Navigating the Transition to RNA-Based Influenza Vaccines: A State-of-the-Art Review.

abstract: SARS-CoV-2 infection causes diverse clinical outcomes, with men facing higher risks of severe disease. Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing mediated by ADAR enzymes governs innate antiviral immunity, yet its contribution to COVID-19 severity and sex-biased disease remains unclear. We performed epitranscriptomic profiling on 126 blood samples from non-COVID controls and COVID-19 patients spanning different disease severities. We detected 1,466 differentially RNA-edited sites in 514 genes linked to clinical outcomes. Although ADAR expression increased in COVID-19 patients overall, it was strongly reduced in ICU patients compared with non-ICU patients, and this shift was far more prominent in males. This severity-associated and sex-biased ADAR/ADARB1 downregulation coincided with decreased global RNA editing and perturbed expression of immune-related edited transcripts. Cathepsin S (CTSS) was identified as a central regulatory node: elevated A-to-I editing within its 3' UTR in ICU patients stabilizes CTSS mRNA. Without stratifying by disease severity, ADAR expression and global editing showed no significant sex differences; the large sex divergence only appeared among ICU patients. This indicates severity-dependent, not infection-innate, disruption of A-to-I editing, disproportionately amplified in critically ill males. CTSS 3'UTR editing may serve as a biomarker for patient stratification, revealing a mechanistic connection between epitranscriptomic changes and male-biased severe COVID-19.

abstract:
AIMS: Eplontersen is an antisense oligonucleotide that suppresses hepatic production of circulating transthyretin (TTR) by targeting TTR mRNA. We present baseline data from an ongoing trial, CARDIO-TTRansform, evaluating eplontersen in patients with TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) and compare findings across previous ATTR-CM trials.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We evaluated 1432 patients enrolled in CARDIO-TTRansform from March 2020 to July 2023 who received ≥1 dose of study intervention (eplontersen or placebo) and had ≥1 post-baseline measurement. Mean (standard deviation) age was 76.4 (7.1) years; 9.4% were female; 88.8% were White. A total of 211 (14.7%) patients had hereditary/variant ATTR-CM (ATTRv-CM); Val122Ile (p.Val142Ile) was the most common genotype (n = 130). Patients spanned New York Heart Association functional classes I (n = 192), II (n = 997), and III (n = 243); 62.6% were National Amyloidosis Centre disease stage 1. Median (interquartile range) N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide was 2025 (1296-3465) pg/ml; n = 51 measured >8500 pg/ml. Median (interquartile range) high-sensitivity troponin T was 50 (35-69) pg/ml and mean left ventricular ejection fraction was 55.7% (9.7%). At baseline, 57.2% were on TTR stabilizer; 18.4% were on sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors.
CONCLUSION: The baseline characteristics of CARDIO-TTRansform were consistent with previous ATTR-CM trials; however, CARDIO-TTRansform evaluated patients with a wide range of disease severity and receiving the contemporary standard of care for ATTR-CM. Overall, blinded baseline data suggest that CARDIO-TTRansform provides a unique opportunity to determine the clinical benefits of eplontersen in a contemporary setting and in clinically relevant subgroups of patients with ATTR-CM.

abstract: Countries with limited water and land resources confront a significant problem due to the growing demand for medicinal plants. These plants are used worldwide to extract and isolate therapeutically important bioactive molecules, known as secondary metabolites. Many medicinal plant species are currently facing significant conservation challenges due to excessive, unregulated harvesting, driven by rapidly growing demand for plant-derived therapies. Soilless farming techniques like hydroponics, aeroponics, and vertical farming offer a sustainable alternative for generating high-quality planting material on a large scale in a considerably shorter period and with less space. Soilless farming revolutionises agriculture and food production, making it particularly well-suited for urban agriculture by reducing maintenance requirements and maximizing crop yields. Soilless farming of numerous medicinal herbs, fruit crops, and vegetables has become increasingly popular in recent years, particularly for its ability to produce large amounts of biomass, high yields, and a wide range of pharmacologically active metabolites. These high-tech systems have significant promise for increased crop yields, cleaner produce, season-independent cultivation, and reduced environmental impact, particularly in water use and disease, compared to traditional soil-based systems. This review article rigorously evaluates recent advancements in soilless agriculture, including LED spectral regulation, nano-elicitation, microbial biostimulants and precursor-feeding strategies, reusable substrates, computational technologies, and CRISPR/Cas-based editing, with respect to their efficacy in generating high-quality plant biomass, improving automation, and optimizing shoot architecture. Implementing soilless farming to produce and synthesize bioactive molecules is expected to be crucial in enhancing sustainability and human well-being.
