abstract: Pathogenic variants in SCN1A are associated with a broad and overlapping spectrum of epilepsies, ranging from febrile seizures and genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) to severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs), most notably Dravet syndrome. SCN1A encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel α-subunit Nav1.1, which has a critical role in inhibitory interneurons. In classical loss-of-function-associated Dravet syndrome, reduced Nav1.1 function contributes to impaired inhibitory neuronal excitability and network hyperexcitability. However, SCN1A-related disorders are mechanistically heterogeneous, with gain-of-function or mixed-function pathogenic variants being associated with clinically distinct phenotypes, including early-onset DEE and familial hemiplegic migraine type 3 (FHM3). This narrative review integrates functional variant classification with genotype-function-phenotype relationships, clinical diagnosis, and phenotype-specific treatment considerations. Particular emphasis is placed on early molecular testing, careful variant interpretation, and the distinction between chronic sodium-channel-blocker avoidance in classical loss-of-function-associated Dravet syndrome and potential mechanism-informed treatment strategies for selected gain-of-function phenotypes. We also summarize emerging SCN1A-targeted approaches, including antisense oligonucleotide therapy, gene activation, and interneuron-targeted gene replacement. A clearer understanding of variant-specific mechanisms and longitudinal clinical features may improve diagnostic precision, individualized management, and the development of disease-modifying therapies for SCN1A-related epilepsies.

title: SCN1A-Related Epilepsies: Clinical Spectrum and Mechanisms.

abstract: Inherited anemias represent a diverse group of genetic disorders characterized by impaired red blood cell production, increased destruction, or abnormal hemoglobin synthesis. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the contemporary clinical landscape, diagnostic workflows, and therapeutic advancements for both major and rare inherited anemias. Major hemoglobinopathies, including thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD), continue to impose a significant global health burden, while rare conditions such as hereditary hemolytic anemias (HHAs), congenital dyserythropoietic anemias (CDAs), and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) present unique diagnostic challenges. Recent years have seen a paradigm shift in laboratory investigations, primarily driven by the integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) and third-generation sequencing (TGS) into clinical practice. These technologies have revolutionized the identification of causative variants, particularly in complex or multiallelic cases that elude traditional biochemical assays. Furthermore, specialized flow cytometry, such as eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding, remains critical for the diagnosis of red cell membrane defects. Therapeutic management is also undergoing a transformation. Beyond traditional supportive care and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), groundbreaking gene-editing therapies, most notably CRISPR/Cas9-mediated BCL11A enhancer editing, offer the potential for curative outcomes in beta-hemoglobinopathies. Novel pharmacological agents, such as luspatercept for thalassemia and mitapivat for pyruvate kinase deficiency, are providing targeted options to improve erythropoiesis and reduce transfusion burden. Despite these advances, challenges remain in ensuring equitable access to these high-cost interventions and addressing the diagnostic gaps in resource-limited settings.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) remains the most aggressive and treatment-refractory primary brain tumor, with current therapeutic modalities providing minimal survival improvement. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapies succeeded in hematologic malignancies but are constrained in solid tumors by tumor heterogeneity, immunosuppressive microenvironment, and delivery challenges. CD276 (B7-H3), a pan-cancer antigen overexpressed in gliomas and correlated with poor patient outcomes, represents a compelling immunotherapeutic target. Methods: Here, we developed a non-viral lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for transient CAR mRNA delivery to T cells and evaluated its application for generating CD276 (B7-H3)-targeted CAR-T cells against GBM. An in-house-assembled T-mixer incorporating polyether ether ketone (PEEK) tubing was integrated with a dual-syringe-pump system for controlled LNP production. Results: LNPs formulated with clinically relevant ionizable lipids, SM-102 and DLin-MC3-DMA, demonstrated high encapsulation efficiency and effective mRNA delivery. Cell-type-dependent expression kinetics were further characterized following LNP-mediated reporter mRNA delivery in K562, NK, NK92, and T cells, revealing differences in transgene expression across cell populations. LNP-mediated delivery of CD276 CAR mRNA enabled generation of CAR-expressing T cells that exhibited antigen-specific cytotoxicity against CD276-positive LN229 GBM cells in vitro. Conclusions: Collectively, this study demonstrates the feasibility of an adaptable LNP-based platform for non-viral CAR mRNA engineering of T cells and CD276-targeted cytotoxicity against GBM cells in vitro. The combination of transient CAR expression and LNP-mediated mRNA delivery provides a foundation for further optimization and evaluation in preclinical in vivo models.

abstract:
An open-label, controlled, multi-site, interventional, 2-arm, Phase II/III trial of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab vs pembrolizumab monotherapy as first line treatment in patients with unresectable recurrent or metastatic HPV16+ HNSCC expressing programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) with combined positive score (CPS) ≥1.

This trial has two parts.

Part A, is an initial non-randomized Safety Run-In Phase to confirm the safety and tolerability at the selected dose range level of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab.

Part B, is a randomized part to generate pivotal efficacy and safety data of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab monotherapy in the first line setting in patients with unresectable recurrent or metastatic HPV16+ HNSCC expressing PD-L1 with CPS ≥1. Patients included in the Safety Run-In Phase of the trial (Part A) will not be randomized to Part B and will continue on-trial treatment (BNT113 plus pembrolizumab) within Part A.

For Part B, an optional pre-screening phase is available for all patients where patients' tumor samples may be submitted for central HPV16 DNA and central PD-L1 expression testing prior to screening into the main trial.

Patients will be treated with BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab or with pembrolizumab monotherapy for approximately up to 24 months.

abstract: Reliable circulating biomarkers for prognosis and treatment monitoring in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain limited. Liquid biopsy offers a minimally invasive approach to identify clinically informative tumour-derived markers. Given the emerging role of GalNAc-transferases in cancer biology, we evaluated GALNT13 expression in peripheral blood as a potential biomarker for prognosis and disease monitoring in lung cancer patients. Sensitive molecular assays (nested and digital RT-PCR) were developed to detect GALNT13 mRNA in circulating tumour cells (CTCs). These methods were applied to peripheral blood samples from non-small cell lung cancer patients to assess prognostic value and enable longitudinal monitoring. A cohort of 143 NSCLC patients was analysed, of whom 60% were GALNT13-positive in peripheral blood at baseline. During a five-year follow-up, GALNT13 positivity was significantly associated with reduced overall survival. In several patients, increases in GALNT13 levels preceded radiologic evidence of disease progression. GALNT13 expression in CTCs emerges as a promising biomarker for prognosis and treatment monitoring in NSCLC. Prospective studies in larger cohorts are warranted to validate its clinical utility.

abstract: SUGP1 (SURP and G-patch domain containing 1) participates in splice-site recognition through its interaction with SF3B1, and loss of this factor leads to aberrant splicing. While its role in pre-mRNA splicing is well-documented, its impact on small RNA pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we used CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SUGP1 editing in Bombyx mori BmE cell populations and RNAi to systemically knock down SUGP1 in Drosophila melanogaster. SUGP1 loss caused widespread splicing abnormalities in both species and reduced transposon-derived piRNA abundance as shown by small RNA-seq. Notably, the expression and splicing patterns of known piRNA pathway genes remained largely unchanged. Integrating silkworm transcriptomic data with the Flag-SUGP1 Co-IP/MS interactome revealed no direct association with the components of the piRNA biogenesis pathway, but identified a physical interaction with the Y-box protein (YBX), suggesting a potential link connecting splicing surveillance to RNA metabolism and proteostasis. Collectively, these correlative findings suggest that SUGP1 depletion perturbs global RNA processing, and piRNA reduction may represent a secondary outcome associated with cellular stress or dysregulated RNA metabolism within these two tested insect systems. These results suggest a potential indirect link between SUGP1-dependent splicing regulation and piRNA abundance in the tested insect models.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Plant mitochondrial genomes are structurally dynamic, and assembled paths may not reflect all molecular configurations. We characterized the mitochondrial genome of Rhododendron spinuliferum and evaluated repeat-associated structural heterogeneity and transcript support for mitochondrial RNA processing. Methods: Public PacBio HiFi reads were assembled and curated; Illumina reads from a second individual provided cross-individual sequence support. Candidate local connections were assessed by strict single-read two-junction phasing. Gene content, repeats, plastid-derived sequences, comparative genomics, phylogeny, predicted C-to-U RNA-editing sites, and mature exon junctions were also examined. Results: Three representative assembly paths totaled 786,593 bp and contained 32 protein-coding loci, three rRNA genes, and 19 tRNA types. A total of 226 HiFi reads supported four local configurations associated with two repeat pairs, and all four persisted across 24 filtering combinations. Nine mitochondrial plastid DNA transfer blocks covered 6.77 kb. Public RNA-seq data provided read-level support for 211 of 475 predicted editing sites and all 12 examined mature exon junctions of nad1, nad2, and nad5. Across six congeners, 99.7% of resolved homologous positions corresponding to RNA-supported sites retained genomic C. Conclusions: These results support repeat-associated local structural heterogeneity in the R. spinuliferum mitogenome and provide a curated DNA- and RNA-supported resource for comparative Rhododendron mitochondrial genomics.

abstract: Background: Infantile hemangioma (IH) is the most common benign vascular tumor of infancy, and propranolol, the current first-line treatment, requires prolonged twice-daily dosing and has adverse systemic effects. Methods: Using the public GSE127487 transcriptomic dataset together with weighted gene coexpression network analysis and protein-protein interaction network analysis, we identified JAG1, a principal endothelial Notch ligand, as the most connected node in the disease protein-protein interaction network, with elevated expression across all clinical stages of IH. To test its use as a drug target, we engineered a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) composed of SM-102/DSPC/cholesterol/DMG-PEG2000 that carried JAG1-specific siRNA. Results: At an N/P ratio of 8, the formulation efficiently encapsulated the siRNA, protected it from serum nucleases, and remained colloidally stable. LNP-mediated JAG1 knockdown reduced Matrigel network formation by hemangioma stem cells in vitro. In a hemangioma xenograft model, the intratumoral delivery of JAG1 siRNA reduced tumor volume by approximately 75%, tumor weight by approximately 80%, and microvessel density by more than half, without overt toxicity to the measures collected (body weight and clinical observation). Conclusions: In this preclinical model, JAG1 emerges as a credible therapeutic target, and LNP-delivered JAG1 siRNA is a promising gene-silencing strategy against IH angiogenesis.

outcomes.description: The primary endpoint is variant-specific immune response (magnitude and breadth) to licensed recombinant and mRNA COVID-19 products administered to adult MHS beneficiaries who are eligible for a fall COVID-19 vaccine and who are not severely immunocompromised. This will include quantifying the magnitude of binding and neutralizing antibodies to the vaccine variants and to the dominant variant present 30 days and 150 days post-vaccination. Specifically, we will test neutralizing titers (defined as the inverse serum dilution causing a 50% reduction in relative light units in a pseudovirus neutralization assay) and IgG binding antibody levels (measured in arbitrary units) against the following SARS-CoV-2 variants: XFG (vaccine strain), Wuhan-1 (ancestral strain), plus the dominant circulating variant(s) circulating during the fall of 2026 and winter of 2026-2027.
outcomes.measure: Variant-specific immune responses
outcomes.time_frame: IgG binding antibody levels and neutralizing antibody titers will be assessed on serum samples obtained just prior to vaccination, 30 days (+/- 10 days), and 150 days (+/- 10 days) after vaccination.

abstract: Nonhematopoietic stromal cells are essential regulators of hematopoiesis; however, their contribution to leukemogenesis and immune dysfunction remains poorly defined. In this study, we identified fibroblast-derived fibroblast growth factor 18 (FGF18) as a novel stromal cytokine that reprograms leukemia-immune interactions. Single-cell RNA sequencing of the bone marrow niche in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) revealed the upregulation of Fgf18 in stromal fibroblasts. Administration of recombinant FGF18 accelerated AML progression, whereas fibroblast-specific Fgf18 depletion markedly delayed disease development and improved the survival of mice. We performed a pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screen in AML cells and identified FGF receptor 3 (FGFR3) signaling as a critical mediator of leukemic fitness in the FGF18-rich microenvironment. Genetic loss of Fgfr3 in AML cells recapitulated the effects of FGF18 deficiency and limited leukemic expansion in vivo. Mechanistically, FGF18 binds to its receptor, FGFR3, on AML cells, activating the protein kinase B (AKT)-mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) (AKT-mTOR) signaling pathway and inducing interleukin-6 (IL-6) production. IL-6 acts autocrinely to reinforce leukemic signaling and paracrinely to activate fibroblast JAK-STAT3 signaling, thereby amplifying stromal fibroblast FGF18 expression and forming a feed-forward loop that suppresses CD8+ T-cell effector function and weakens antileukemic immunity. Clinically, elevated FGF18 expression correlates with poor prognosis in patients with AML. To therapeutically target this malignant cross talk, we generated an FGF18-neutralizing antibody that disrupted the stromal-leukemia feedback loop, restored CD8+ T cell effector function, and synergized with anti-PD-1 therapy to elicit durable antileukemic immunity in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify an FGF18-dependent stromal-leukemia cross talk axis that drives AML progression and immune dysfunction, highlighting FGF18 neutralization as a potential therapeutic strategy.

abstract: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a global public health burden, and functional cure represents the primary goal of clinical management. The nuclear covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) minichromosome stably maintained in infected hepatocytes constitutes the major barrier to HBV cure. Clinically, functional cure is defined as sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seroclearance with undetectable serum HBV DNA after finite treatment, a definition that does not require complete cccDNA elimination. At the molecular level, functional cure is thought to be associated with stable transcriptional silencing of cccDNA and integrated HBV DNA, a state biologically distinct from physical cccDNA depletion. Accumulating data demonstrate that the persistence and transcriptional homeostasis of the cccDNA reservoir are controlled by viral proteins and dynamically shaped by host metabolic signaling and epigenetic remodeling. Here, we first outline key steps of the HBV life cycle to establish the mechanistic context for cccDNA formation and replenishment, and then focus our synthesis on the integrated host metabolic-epigenetic network that governs cccDNA establishment, transcriptional activity, stability, and clearance. We dissect how central carbon metabolites, bile acid signaling, histone post-translational modifications, and immune cytokines converge to modulate cccDNA reservoir homeostasis, and critically evaluate the strength of evidence supporting their physiological relevance in the chronically infected human liver. We also discuss mechanisms of HBV immune evasion, including hepatitis B virus X protein (HBx)-driven epigenetic reprogramming and subviral particle-associated immune tolerance. We summarize preclinical and clinical therapeutic strategies targeting the metabolic-epigenetic microenvironment, viral assembly, antigen secretion, and cccDNA modulation to achieve a functional cure for HBV infection. Finally, we outline key unresolved challenges in the field, including the undefined in vivo cccDNA turnover kinetics, the poorly characterized physiological relevance of cell-to-cell transmission, the inherent limitations of gene-editing technologies, and the urgent need for specific non-invasive biomarkers reflecting intrahepatic cccDNA activity.

title: Metabolic-epigenetic regulation of the HBV cccDNA reservoir: pathways underpinning viral persistence.

abstract: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a major cause of chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal failure, involving progressive damage to renal cells, including podocytes. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as important mediators of intercellular communication in the kidney by transporting bioactive molecules such as non-coding RNAs. Rab3A, a small GTPase involved in vesicle docking and fusion at the plasma membrane, may influence EV biogenesis and the cargo composition. This study investigated the non-coding RNA content of EVs released by podocytes following RAB3A silencing under diabetic conditions. Cultured podocytes were transfected with RAB3A-specific siRNA and exposed to high glucose concentrations. EVs were isolated from culture media and characterized using complementary techniques, and their non-coding RNA cargo was analyzed via high-throughput sequencing and validated via RT-qPCR. Our results reveal that RAB3A silencing under high-glucose conditions induced significant changes in EV-associated non-coding RNAs, including altered levels of miR-126-3p. The context-dependent regulation of miR-126-3p suggests its involvement in IRS1/PI3K-Akt signaling, potentially affecting the balance between protective and pathogenic responses in the diabetic kidney. Overall, these findings provide new insights into the role of Rab3A in shaping EV cargo during diabetic stress and highlight EV-associated non-coding RNAs as potential contributors to the pathophysiology of DN.

abstract: The worldwide opioid epidemic continues to claim thousands of lives each year and remains one of the most urgent global public health challenges, driven by the high abuse potential and overdose risk of potent, fully synthetic μ-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists such as fentanyl. While fentanyl is highly effective in pain management, it also carries severe risks including respiratory depression, addiction, and fatal overdose. Understanding the neurobiological pathways underlying these risks is essential for developing safer analgesics and effective interventions. The MOR, a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that modulates neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission in important brain circuits like the ventral tegmental area (VTA), nucleus accumbens (NAc), and prefrontal cortex (PFC), is the primary receptor through which opioids exert their therapeutic effects. Dopaminergic dysregulation, transcriptional remodeling, and altered synaptic plasticity are neuroadaptations brought on by long-term opioid exposure that contribute to dependence and relapse. Life-threatening opioid toxicity is primarily driven by MOR-mediated suppression of respiratory networks, with risk shaped by dose, pharmacokinetics, receptor efficacy, and circuit sensitivity. Zebrafish (Danio rerio) provide a powerful complementary system for dissecting opioid-related neurocircuitry and screening for potential therapeutics. Zebrafish share conserved opioid-signaling components with mammals, and larval transparency facilitates in vivo imaging of neuronal activity at cellular resolution. Behavioral paradigms capture reward-related and drug-seeking phenotypes, while CRISPR-based approaches offer a means to investigate receptor-specific functions in validated models. In addition, zebrafish larvae provide an efficient platform for high-throughput screening of compounds that modulate opioid signaling and respiratory-related phenotypes. Together, insights from human, rodent, and zebrafish studies provide a more integrated understanding of opioid overdose and addiction neurobiology. This review incorporates current knowledge on the molecular and circuit-level mechanisms driving these processes and discusses how zebrafish models accelerate the discovery of safer analgesics and novel treatments for opioid use disorder and overdose.

abstract: Chromosomal abnormalities are among the most common molecular characteristics of human cancer cells and are believed to play an essential role in the genesis of tumor driver molecules. Chromosome translocations are one of the first recognized tumor-related chromatin alterations; many of them are so typical to certain neoplasms that they are used as diagnostic biomarkers in contemporary clinical histopathology. Understanding their molecular roles in carcinogenesis is essential to the development of novel targeted therapeutics but this has been hindered by the difficulties in establishing appropriate in vitro models. Here, we review the recent advances of the field covering its historical background, medical relevance and most recent technological breakthroughs in chromosomal translocation modeling that may facilitate the innovations of related tumor-agnostic therapeutic modalities.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by extensive neural remodeling and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, both of which contribute to disease progression and therapeutic resistance. However, whether nociceptor-derived signals directly reprogram PDAC cells to promote immune evasion remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized tumor-intrinsic neuroimmune mechanism driven by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) signaling through the receptor complex RAMP1/CALCRL on PDAC cells. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of Ramp1 or Calcrl did not alter PDAC cell proliferation in vitro but markedly suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in immunocompetent mice. These antitumor effects were lost in immunodeficient hosts, indicating that the pro-tumorigenic function of CGRP signaling depends on an intact host immune system. Consistently, tumor cell-specific loss of Ramp1 or Calcrl remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment, enhancing CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell effector activity. Mechanistically, CGRP stimulation promoted TGF-β2 expression and secretion by PDAC cells in a RAMP1-dependent manner. Tumor-derived TGF-β2 subsequently acted in a paracrine fashion to suppress CD8+ T-cell activation and cytotoxic function, whereas genetic disruption of RAMP1 or pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling relieved this immunosuppression. Together, these findings define a CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL-TGF-β2 signaling axis through which nociceptive input is converted into tumor-driven adaptive immune evasion in PDAC. This pathway reveals a previously underappreciated mechanism linking neural signaling to PDAC progression and identifies CGRP receptor signaling as a potential therapeutic vulnerability for restoring antitumor immunity and improving the responsiveness of PDAC to immunotherapy.

title: CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL Signaling Drives TGF-β2-Mediated Immune Evasion and Pancreatic Cancer Progression.

abstract: Developing new cancer therapeutic strategies has become a central focus in precision oncology. However, a major challenge is the lack of robust models to accurately assess target vulnerability in patient-specific heterogeneous cancer cells, which limits the translation of research findings into effective clinical therapies. In this study, we developed an ex vivo blood-based model utilizing a versatile nano-delivery platform to evaluate the responsiveness of MDM2 knockout as a representative therapeutic approach in circulating malignant cells (CMCs) from patients stratified by their p53 status. In our genome editing plasmid delivery system (p@RPA), protamine sulfate was combined with a cell-penetrating peptide to condense the CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid into nano-cores. These nano-cores were then coated with chondroitin sulfate shells functionalized with the AS1411 aptamer, enabling the selective recognition of CD44 and/or nucleolin overexpressing malignant cells. Using the same vector, a molecular beacon delivery system (MBs@RPA) co-loaded with MBMDM2 for probing MDM2 mRNA, MBTP53 for probing TP53 mRNA and MBTP73 for probing TP73 mRNA was constructed for the in situ evaluation of biomarker changes induced by genome editing. p@RPA demonstrates satisfactory efficacy in mediating gene editing for MDM2 knockout in malignant cells. Notably, the knockout of MDM2 induces cell cycle arrest and leads to a marked upregulation of anti-tumor TAp73 irrespective of their p53 status. With efficient gene editing and mRNA probing achieved in patient-derived CMCs, we establish an ex vivo platform capable of in situ therapeutic efficacy assessment at single-cell resolution to explicitly reveal the underlying cellular heterogeneity across individual CMCs.

title: A targeting delivery platform for the mapping of responses to p53-independent intervention in heterogeneous patient cancer cells.

abstract: Screening for high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is a pivotal strategy for the prevention of invasive cervical cancer, particularly in resource-constrained settings. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-based compact automated real-time detection system, termed Ccard, for rapid testing of HPV16, HPV18, and the internal reference gene GAPDH through a streamlined workflow. A simple room-temperature treatment efficiently releases nucleic acids directly from swab samples, bypassing the need for extraction. The mixture was driven through the channels and loaded into the reaction chambers on the microfluidic chip by a vacuum pump. The lyophilized reagents in the reaction zone of the microfluidic chip were redissolved. The system subsequently performs a single-step RPA-CRISPR/Cas13a reaction, with real-time detection enabled by an Internet of Things device. The assay achieved detection within 30 min, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 5 copies/µL for both HPV16 and HPV18. Validation with clinical samples demonstrated high sensitivity (96.8% for HPV16 and 100% for HPV18) and 100% specificity. These results highlight the reliability, precision, and strong potential of the Ccard system for rapid testing of HR-HPVs.

title: Integrated Microfluidic CRISPR-Based Diagnostic Device for Rapid Testing of HPVs.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) is the most common endocrine malignancy and is generally associated with favorable clinical outcomes. However, a subset of tumors develops aggressive phenotypes characterized by increased proliferation, migration, therapeutic resistance, and disease progression. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as important regulators of tumor biology, yet the role of Long Intergenic Non-Protein Coding RNA 1614 (LINC01614) in PTC remains poorly understood. This study investigated the functional role of LINC01614 in PTC and its potential involvement in ferroptosis-associated molecular pathways. Methods: RNA sequencing data from a repository of 44 paired PTC and adjacent normal thyroid tissue samples were analyzed to identify differentially expressed lncRNAs. LINC01614 expression was evaluated in thyroid cell lines, and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) was used to generate stable LINC01614 knockdown K1 cell lines. Cellular proliferation, migration, clonogenicity, intracellular iron accumulation, lipid peroxidation, cytokine secretion, and ferroptosis-associated gene expression were assessed using qRT-PCR, RNA sequencing, Western blotting, cytokine array analysis, iron quantification assays, and BODIPY C11 lipid peroxidation imaging. Results: LINC01614 was significantly overexpressed in PTC tissues and thyroid cancer cell lines. CRISPRi-mediated repression of LINC01614 reduced cellular proliferation, migration, and clonogenic capacity. Mechanistically, LINC01614 knockdown resulted in an 8.8-fold increase in miR-4521 expression and a 23-fold decrease in IGF2 expression, supporting a potential competing endogenous RNA mechanism. Reduced LINC01614 expression was associated with decreased AKT, GPX4, SLC7A11, and SLC3A2 expression, increased IL-6 secretion, a 3.4-fold increase in intracellular ferrous iron accumulation, and a marked increase in lipid peroxidation following erastin treatment, indicating enhanced sensitivity to ferroptosis. Conclusions: These findings identify LINC01614 as a novel regulator of aggressive PTC phenotypes and ferroptosis resistance. The data support a model in which LINC01614 contributes to thyroid cancer progression through modulation of a miR-4521/IGF2/PI3K/AKT signaling axis and downstream anti-ferroptotic pathways. LINC01614 may represent a promising biomarker and potential therapeutic target in papillary thyroid cancer.

title: Long Non-Coding RNA LINC01614 Promotes Aggressive Phenotypes and Ferroptosis Resistance in Papillary Thyroid Cancer Through a Putative miR-4521/IGF2/PI3K-AKT Signaling Axis.

abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most prevalent malignancies of the gastrointestinal tract worldwide. Notably, most patients with microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumors show primary resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), creating an unmet clinical need. The mechanisms underlying immune evasion and strategies to overcome therapeutic resistance have therefore become important topics in CRC immunology research. Recent studies indicate that mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion in CRC. Tumor cells display metabolic plasticity through dynamic shifts between glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), which can intensify the depletion of critical nutrients, particularly glucose and glutamine, within the tumor microenvironment (TME). These metabolic changes can also promote the accumulation of immunosuppressive metabolites, including lactate, thereby impairing the function of effector cells such as CD8+ T cells and dendritic cells (DCs) and supporting the expansion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Lactate may further reshape the immune landscape through hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 1 (HCAR1) signaling and histone lactylation. In parallel, mitochondrial quality control can regulate tumor immunogenicity by influencing mtDNA availability and cGAS-STING signaling. Therapeutic approaches targeting glycolysis, glutamine metabolism, fatty acid oxidation, lactate transport, and mitochondrial dynamics have shown immune-sensitizing activity in preclinical models. Nanodelivery systems and gene-editing technologies may improve the spatial and cellular specificity of these interventions. This review summarizes how mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion in CRC and evaluates mitochondria-directed strategies for improving treatment responsiveness, particularly in MSS CRC.

title: Mitochondrial Metabolic Reprogramming and Immune Evasion in Colorectal Cancer: Research Advances and Mechanistic Perspectives.

abstract: There is growing interest in natural bioactive compounds as potentially safer and more sustainable sources of therapeutic agents. Terpenoids, one of the most structurally diverse and biologically active classes of natural products, are derived from repeating isoprene units and possess a broad range of pharmacological and industrial applications. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in terpenoid biosynthesis, structural classification, and therapeutic applications. It also discusses emerging approaches for enhancing large-scale production, improving functional efficacy, and overcoming pharmacokinetic limitations. Attention is given to terpenoids currently undergoing clinical evaluation, along with their progress toward commercial development. Despite substantial preclinical evidence supporting their therapeutic potential, the clinical translation of many terpenoids remains limited. Key challenges include poor aqueous solubility, low permeability, slow dissolution, and high lipophilicity, which can collectively restrict systemic bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, only a relatively small proportion of biologically active terpenoids have progressed to advanced stages of clinical development, highlighting a considerable gap between experimental findings and clinical application. This review integrates current knowledge of terpenoid biosynthesis, biological activities, production strategies, and translational development while highlighting sustainable and scientifically driven approaches that may facilitate their future therapeutic and commercial utilization.

title: Terpenoids: A Comprehensive Review on Biosynthesis, Applications and Enhancement Strategies for Translational Research.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance is increasingly strained by interconnected global crises, i.e., pandemics, climate change, armed conflicts, population mobility, and health inequalities, that disrupt healthcare delivery, diagnostic capacity, and laboratory infrastructure. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, whole-genome sequencing, metagenomics, and digital surveillance offer the potential to shift from reactive reporting to predictive intelligence that anticipates resistance threats, although current implementations remain sector-specific, retrospective, and project-funded. Environmental surveillance, particularly wastewater monitoring coupled with genomic epidemiology, provides early warnings at population and ecosystem levels. The future integration of AI across human, animal, and environmental sectors could enable unified One Health intelligence; no such integrated platform is currently operational. This review focuses primarily on bacterial AMR. It examines how global drivers strain surveillance, how genomic, metagenomic, digital, and AI-enabled technologies reshape AMR detection and prediction, and the emerging non-antibiotic therapeutic landscape, including bacteriophage therapy, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, microbiota-directed interventions, nanomedicine, host-directed therapies, photodynamic therapy, and vaccines. It then explores how these innovations can be integrated within a One Health framework to support coordinated global preparedness. Addressing the AMR crisis will require not only technological innovation but also equitable implementation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and resilient systems.

title: Surveillance, Detection and Therapeutic Innovation in Antimicrobial Resistance in the Age of Polycrisis: From Genomic and Digital Innovation to One Health Integration.

abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication depends on a complex interplay between viral proteins and host cellular factors, which represent promising therapeutic targets. However, systematic integration of results from genome-wide CRISPR screens for HIV host factors remains limited. Here, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens to identify host dependency, restriction, and latency-promoting factors in HIV-1 infection. Following PRISMA guidelines, we identified 11 eligible studies from which we extracted 26 gene lists. These were classified into three phenotypic categories, including dependency (5 lists), restriction (10 lists), and latency-promoting (7 lists), and integrated using meta-analysis by information content (MAIC). GO over-representation analysis and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis were performed on MAIC-ranked gene lists to characterize pathway architectures. MAIC successfully recovered well-established host factors, including the entry receptors CD4, CCR5, and CXCR4; the integration cofactor PSIP1 (LEDGF/p75); and the restriction factors TRIM5, TRIM22, PML, G3BP1, and EIF2AK2. RNF114 emerged as the top-ranked restriction factor, supported by four independent publication-level categories. Additional high-confidence hits included TRIM56, BIRC3, DTX3L, and components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system across the dependency and latency datasets, further supporting the robustness of the MAIC framework. Beyond these canonical factors, we identified multiple undercharacterized genes and pathways, including coagulation and IL-17 signaling in dependency factors, SUMOylation and DNA damage response in restriction factors, and the Integrator complex and proteasome-granule co-enrichment in latency-promoting factors. Leading-edge analysis confirmed that most of these non-canonical enrichments are driven by coherent gene modules rather than a small set of pleiotropic hubs. These findings reveal distinct pathway architectures across the three infection states and highlight previously unrecognized host processes that may serve as targets for antiviral therapy. Our analysis provides a comprehensive resource for guiding future mechanistic studies of host-HIV interactions and developing strategies to enhance immunity, block viral replication, and reverse latency.

outcomes.description: The PHQ-9 is a 9-question screening tool used to assess depression severity. Each of the 9 items evaluates symptoms over the last 2 weeks and is scored from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day), resulting in a total possible score ranging from 0 to 27. Higher scores indicate higher depression severity.
outcomes.measure: Change in Physical Health Questionnaire depression scale (PHQ-9)
outcomes.time_frame: Baseline, 1 week, 2 weeks, 3 weeks, 4 weeks, 3 months

outcomes.description: The GAD-7 is a 7-item tool used to screen for Generalized Anxiety Disorder and assess symptom severity. Respondents rate how often they've been bothered by anxiety symptoms over the past two weeks on a scale of 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day). Total scores range from 0 to 21, where higher scores indicate greater levels of anxiety.
outcomes.measure: Change in Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) score
outcomes.time_frame: Baseline, 1 week, 2 weeks, 3 weeks, 4 weeks, 3 months

abstract: Articular cartilage repair remains a major clinical challenge due to the limited regenerative capacity of the tissue and the poor therapeutic efficacy of current treatments. Although stem cell-based therapies hold promise, their clinical outcomes are often compromised by insufficient chondrogenic differentiation, phenotypic instability, and rapid cell loss in the dynamic joint environment. Herein, we report an ultrasound-responsive, bio-scaffold system (e-BMSCs/Gel) designed to enhance cartilage regeneration through coordinated biochemical and genetic regulation. In this system, bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) are engineered by internalizing nanobubbles (NBs) loaded with TGF-β3 protein and CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids targeting the YAP (pCas9-YAP), termed T@NBspDNA. Additionally, to enhance cell retention and survival, engineered BMSCs (e-BMSCs) are encapsulated within a thermosensitive thiolated-chitosan/hydroxyapatite hydrogel that rapidly forms in situ. Under US stimulation, the synchronized activation of TGF-β3 release and YAP gene silencing significantly promoted the chondrogenic differentiation of e-BMSCs. Furthermore, in vivo evaluation in a rat articular cartilage defect model demonstrates that US-activated e-BMSCs/Gel effectively promotes hyaline-like cartilage regeneration and improves structural restoration of the defect site. Overall, this work presents a controllable bio-scaffold platform, offering a novel strategy for effective cartilage regeneration.

abstract: Zebrafish is an excellent in vivo model for high-throughput antiangiogenic drug testing, commonly known as the zebrafish angiogenesis assay. Conventional zebrafish angiogenesis assays are performed in wild-type zebrafish to evaluate the vascular changes in intersegmental and subintestinal vessel regions of the zebrafish larvae at 2 and 3 dpf stages, respectively. However, wild-type zebrafish larvae do not adequately mimic the hypoxia microenvironment and ectopic vessel branching characteristics of cancer. To overcome this limitation, we developed a genetically engineered zebrafish model with constitutive activation of the hypoxia signaling pathway by targeting the vhl, a tumor suppressor, by negative regulation of the hypoxia pathway, using CRISPR mutagenesis. This model exhibits robust ectopic blood vessel branching throughout the larval body, thereby recapitulating pathological angiogenesis. The utility of this zebrafish model system for drug screening was validated with the sorafenib treatment, a known antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Overall, this proangiogenic hypoxia zebrafish model provides a physiologically relevant platform for testing antiangiogenic drugs. Key features • Generate a vhl mutant zebrafish line with constitutive activation of the hypoxia signaling pathway using CRISPR-CAS9 mutagenesis. • The generated model exhibits extensive ectopic neovascular branching and abnormal vascular growth resembling pathological angiogenesis observed in solid tumors. • Mimics the chronic hypoxic microenvironment commonly associated with cancer progression and angiogenesis. • Provides an economical alternative to mammalian tumor models for early-stage antiangiogenic drug testing.

abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel β2-subunit (Navβ2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navβ2V173A,V175K mice with selective reduction of the Navβ2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navβ2V173A,V175K mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navβ2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains a major threat to the global swine industry, while the emergence of variant pseudorabies virus (PRV) strains has further complicated disease control in China. This study aimed to develop a PRV-based viral vector platform for PRRSV antigen delivery and evaluate its safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy. Methods: A five-gene-deleted variant PRV strain, PRV-JM-DF, was used as the vector backbone. Candidate genomic insertion sites and endogenous late promoters were systematically screened, followed by construction of recombinant PRVs expressing PRRSV GP2, GP3, GP4, GP5, and M individually or as tandem antigen constructs. Recombinant viruses were characterized for antigen expression, replication, and genetic stability. Safety and immunogenicity were initially evaluated in female BALB/c mice, and the leading candidates were further assessed for safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy in 18 Landrace pigs of either sex following challenge with highly pathogenic PRRSV HuN4. Results: The TK locus supported efficient foreign-gene expression, and pUL39 exhibited the highest activity among the tested endogenous late promoters. The recombinant viruses retained replication competence and genetic stability. Among the candidates, rPRV-C-4T induced robust PRRSV- and PRV-specific neutralizing antibody responses and showed no obvious adverse effects during the experimental observation period in pigs. Following HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge, all rPRV-C-4T-immunized pigs survived and exhibited reduced viremia, viral shedding and tissue viral loads, together with markedly alleviated pathological lesions. Conclusions: rPRV-C-4T provided protection against homologous HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge while maintaining PRV-directed immune responses, supporting its potential as a PRV-vectored multivalent vaccine candidate.

title: Construction of Recombinant PRV Expressing PRRSV Antigens and Evaluation of Their Protective Efficacy in Pigs Against Homologous Challenge.

abstract: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is the most common inherited retinal dystrophy and remains largely untreatable. This review summarizes RP pathogenesis and critically appraises emerging therapeutic strategies, including gene augmentation, gene editing, RNA-based therapies, gene-agnostic and neuroprotective approaches, stem-cell therapy and their delivery platforms. We compare these strategies according to mutation mechanism, disease stage, durability, delivery route, and current level of clinical evidence. Although several approaches have shown improved structural and functional outcomes in preclinical and early-phase studies, RPE65-directed gene augmentation (voretigen neparvovec) remains the only approved therapy, and even it does not halt degeneration. For most modalities, long-term efficacy, safety, durability and clinical validation are not yet established, and translation is further constrained by delivery, immunogenicity, manufacturing, and cost. Rather than a realized paradigm shift, current evidence points to a rapidly advancing but still largely investigational field with successful clinical translation remaining elusive.

title: Cancer cells hijack mitochondria from Bhlhe40+ T cells for immune evasion

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major global health problem. Functional cure is defined as sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seroclearance with undetectable HBV DNA 24 weeks after cessation of therapy. It has emerged as a clinically meaningful endpoint, associated with regression of liver fibrosis, reduced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk, and a lower treatment burden. However, current CHB therapies, including nucleos(t)ide analogues (NUCs) and pegylated interferon-α (Peg-IFNα), rarely lead to functional cure despite adequate viral suppression, leading to a notable portion of patients remaining at risk for adverse liver-related outcomes, including hepatic decompensation and HCC. Hence, novel therapeutic agents are aimed at accelerating towards functional cure. They are categorized as virus-targeting and immunomodulatory therapies.
METHODS: This review summarizes the clinical evidence for emerging therapies aimed at acheiving functional cure, with a particular focus on RNA-targeting therapies. It also discusses practical considerations relevant to treatment selection.
RESULTS: Among these novel therapies, RNA-targeting therapies are currently the most promising, with bepirovirsen (an unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide) standing out as the only agent completed in Phase III study showing efficacious results. Combination regimens that use RNA-targeting therapies as backbone are increasingly pursued, leveraging potential synergistic effects to achieve higher rates of HBsAg seroclearance.
CONCLUSION: RNA-targetting therapies and combination regimens offer promising approaches in attaining functional cure in CHB. Further research should emphasize on the long-term efficacy and safety for these novel agents.

title: Clinical Prospect of Novel Therapies for Functional Cure in Chronic Hepatitis B.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved remarkable remission rates exceeding 80% in relapsed/refractory pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), yet 40-50% of patients eventually relapse within the first year. This therapeutic ceiling is not a single failure mode but the convergence of at least four interrelated layers: loss of CAR-T persistence, antigen escape driven by CD19 splicing variants and lineage switch, CAR-T cell-intrinsic exhaustion from chronic tonic signaling, and an immunosuppressive bone marrow microenvironment that actively extinguishes effector function. Our systematic analysis of 226 pediatric-eligible CAR-T trials shows that 95.6% are Phase I-II, 3.5% (8/226) are registered as Phase III/IV, and 58 of 102 completed trials (56.9%) had no outcome recorded in the source database. In this Perspective, we synthesize the molecular mechanisms of CAR-T resistance, contextualize them within the current clinical trial landscape, and critically evaluate emerging engineering strategies-from dual-targeting and armored CAR architectures to CRISPR-edited allogeneic products and in vivo mRNA delivery. We argue that progress depends on both smarter receptor design and structural reforms in trial design, outcome transparency and global collaboration.

title: Resistance mechanisms and translational bottlenecks in CAR-T cell therapy for pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia: a perspective.

abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines are detectable in human blood after vaccination, but platform-specific differences in systemic persistence and transcript integrity remain poorly defined. We analyzed serial blood samples from 73 participants receiving Moderna mRNA-1273 (three formulations), Pfizer/BioNTech BNT162b2, or an investigational receptor-binding domain (RBD) mRNA vaccine (three different doses). Using droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) assays, we quantified total and long-range linked ("intact") vaccine mRNA, and we measured vaccine-specific ionizable lipids by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Across platforms, mRNA decay was fastest for mRNA-1273, intermediate for BNT162b2, and slowest for the RBD vaccine, with ionizable lipid decay following the same rank order. Notably, intact spike mRNA declined 2-fold faster after mRNA-1273 than BNT162b2 vaccination. Kinetics modeling revealed platform-dependent coupling of mRNA and lipid kinetics: intact mRNA tracked closely with SM-102 for mRNA-1273, whereas ALC-0315 persisted longer than intact mRNA for BNT162b2. A ten-fragment linkage ddPCR panel spanning the spike transcript showed lower linkage toward 3'-proximal regions that mirrored the administered mRNA-1273 formulation. Together, these data provide a quantitative framework for benchmarking mRNA-LNP platform kinetics and transcript integrity in humans.

abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases remain largely untreatable at the disease-modifying level, with currently approved therapies providing primarily symptomatic benefits. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality because of its ability to selectively silence disease-associated genes. However, a major obstacle to clinical translation is not the gene-silencing mechanism itself, but the efficient delivery of therapeutic siRNAs to target cells within the central nervous system.This review examines the barriers that limit siRNA-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. We adopt a barrier-oriented framework that follows the sequential challenges encountered during siRNA delivery, including extracellular instability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, immune recognition, limited transport across the blood-brain barrier, inefficient cellular internalization, and endosomal entrapment. Rather than cataloguing available delivery systems, we evaluate how nanocarrier engineering strategies have been developed to address these barriers and assess their impact on delivery. Evidence from Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease is synthesized to distinguish shared limitations from disease-specific challenges and to evaluate the translational performance of lipid-based nanoparticles, polymeric nanocarriers, engineered exosomes, and hybrid platforms.Available evidence indicates that delivery platforms can improve specific aspects of siRNA transport but have not consistently overcome the sequential biological barriers required for therapy. Although nanocarrier engineering has enhanced siRNA stability, brain targeting, intracellular trafficking, and gene-silencing efficiency in preclinical models, manufacturing scalability, biological heterogeneity, long-term safety, reproducibility, and regulatory feasibility remain important barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will likely depend on delivery systems that integrate effective brain transport, endosomal escape, controlled intracellular release, and scalable manufacturing within clinical platforms.

title: Why does siRNA delivery still fail in neurodegenerative diseases? Biological barriers, nanocarrier engineering, and future translational directions.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells combine innate cytotoxicity with antigen-directed killing and promise as an immunotherapy with lower cytokine toxicity than CAR-T approaches. However, clinical translation is limited by challenges in transduction, persistence, tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed a comprehensive literature review of recent preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, engineering strategies (CAR design, transduction technologies, gene-editing), manufacturing and expansion protocols, and trial outcomes in this review. We noted a reference to the advantages of CAR-NK, like multimodal killing (CAR-dependent and innate pathways), potential for allogeneic "off-the-shelf" use, and favorable early safety profiles. However, NK-specific obstacles persist: lower viral transduction efficiencies, short in vivo persistence, poor infiltration into solid tumors, and TME-mediated suppression (TGF-β, adenosine, metabolic stress). Engineering countermeasures such as IL-15 expression, checkpoint receptor knockout, chemokine receptor co-expression (e.g., CXCR1/4), DAP10/DAP12-based signaling domains, and non-viral delivery (transposons/CRISPR) have shown preclinical promise. CAR-NK therapy has developed from concept to a clinically actionable treatment line for hematologic malignancies and shows emerging potential in solid tumors when combined with TME-modulating strategies. This review provides robust evidence about CAR-NK therapies in hematological and solid tumors, with a great emphasis on the challenges they encounter, strategies, and innovative approaches to overcome these challenges, and forward-looking perspectives to improve future therapeutic CAR-NK designs and clinical outcomes.

abstract: Efficient, biocompatible, and flexible application of CRISPR-Cas9 remains a major challenge in gene therapy. This study addresses a novel formulation method, focusing on organic solvent-free lipid nanoparticles for the efficient delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 components. Therefore, novel stealth lipids comprising the lipid anchor cholesterol hemisuccinate conjugated to poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx) were synthesized and evaluated as a promising in vitro alternative to commercially available poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based lipids. Our study identified PEtOx-lipids as markedly more biocompatible compared to PEG-based analogues (12-fold reduction in cytotoxicity; 99% reduced hemolytic effect) with high efficiency for mRNA gene delivery. We demonstrate successful CRISPR-Cas9 activity ex vivo and efficient uptake of PEtOx nanoparticles by macrophages in vivo (66.5% pos. F4/80+ macrophages). Our data demonstrate that PEtOx-based stealth lipids are a promising alternative to PEG. The resulting LNPs, optimized for fully aqueous manufacturing, address key limitations of current LNP systems, including immunogenicity and the reliance on ethanol-based production processes.

abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4 and CD8 T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever.

abstract: ATP1A3-related neurological disorders comprise a rapidly expanding spectrum of rare neurogenetic diseases characterized by remarkable clinical heterogeneity and complex genotype-phenotype relationships. Since the publication of previous comprehensive reviews, the identification of novel ATP1A3-associated phenotypes, refinement of genotype-phenotype correlations, and advances in molecular pathogenesis and precision therapeutic strategies have substantially expanded current understanding of these disorders, highlighting the need for an updated synthesis. This narrative review summarizes recent advances in the clinical spectrum of ATP1A3-related disorders and discusses current insights into genotype-phenotype correlations, molecular mechanisms, and disease pathogenesis. Particular emphasis is placed on the molecular consequences of ATP1A3 dysfunction, including impaired Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, disrupted neuronal excitability, altered ion homeostasis, and downstream cellular responses. We further review current symptomatic management and emerging disease-modifying therapeutic strategies, including antisense oligonucleotide therapy, viral vector-mediated gene delivery, genome editing technologies, and other precision medicine approaches. Current challenges and future research priorities are also discussed. By integrating recent clinical and experimental evidence, this review provides an updated perspective on ATP1A3-related disorders and aims to facilitate improved disease recognition, mechanistic understanding, and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.

abstract: Spherical nucleic acids (SNAs) are a unique class of nucleic acid nanotherapeutics characterized by densely packed, radially arranged oligonucleotides surrounding a nanoparticle or molecular core, or core-free nanoscale structures. Compared with conventional linear nucleic acids, SNAs exhibit excellent cellular uptake, resistance to nuclease degradation, and efficient target recognition without the help of transfection agents. This review summarizes SNAs' structural diversity, design principles, and the multiscale delivery barriers they encounter. We mainly focus on liposomal SNAs (LSNAs) as programmable platforms for cancer immunotherapy. We emphasize how lipid chemistry, membrane architecture, and anchor stability control lymphoid distribution, immune-cell uptake, antigen presentation, and strong antitumor immunity, rather than seeing lipids as inert carriers. Furthermore, we also discuss current developments in gene silencing, CRISPR-based genome editing, and stimulus-responsive multimodal therapies, highlighting the significant therapeutic advancements of SNAs like clinical trial NU-0129 and LSNAs like cavrotolimod. Finally, we describe present translational obstacles and potential prospects by using SNAs as next-generation precision immunotherapeutics.

abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) represents the most prevalent neurological complication arising from sepsis, affecting approximately 70% of patients with sepsis and associated with mortality rates reaching up to 70%. Survivors frequently experience persistent cognitive deficits; however, the field currently lacks specific diagnostic biomarkers and targeted therapeutic interventions, with diagnosis primarily established through exclusion criteria. This review critically examines multi-omic investigations of SAE, evaluating whether convergent evidence across genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic domains elucidates shared pathophysiological mechanisms and identifying prevailing translational challenges. The synthesis of evidence is structured around three interrelated thematic domains. First, multi-omic analyses have elucidated the initial triggers of neuroinflammation: genomic studies implicate Piezo1-mediated oligodendrocyte ferroptosis and adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing, while proteomic data corroborate activation of the reactive oxygen species (ROS)/thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP)/NLRP3 inflammasome axis, collectively indicating that peripheral inflammatory cues converge upon central innate immune pathways. Second, transcriptomic and proteomic findings converge on microglial polarization as a pivotal mediator in SAE progression: single-cell sequencing reveals C1q-dependent synaptic pruning, S100A9 protein expression promotes pro-inflammatory microglial polarization, and metabolomic profiles demonstrate that cyclophilin D (CypD)-regulated redox imbalances modulate the magnitude of glial inflammatory responses. Third, integrative analyses delineate neuronal injury pathways: the NAT10 (N-acetyltransferase 10)/GABA(B) receptor 1 axis is implicated in inhibitory synaptic dysfunction through coordinated transcriptomic and proteomic alterations, while elevated levels of 4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid correlate with impaired consciousness, suggesting its potential utility as a prognostic biomarker. Across these domains-initiation, mediation, and injury-multi-omic integration further extends the conceptual framework to encompass systemic regulation via the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Notwithstanding these advances, extant evidence is limited by predominantly cross-sectional study designs, reliance on single-animal models, and a paucity of rigorous clinical validation. To address these limitations, we propose a three-tiered cascade model-comprising Inflammation Initiation, Glial Mediation, and Neuronal Injury-that synthesizes current findings into a coherent, testable framework. Furthermore, we delineate a methodological roadmap emphasizing longitudinal sampling, multi-center validation, causal inference methodologies, and artificial intelligence-driven data integration. This review endeavors not only to consolidate existing knowledge but also to establish an actionable translational paradigm aimed at advancing SAE research from descriptive characterization toward precision diagnostics and mechanism-based therapeutic strategies.

abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is characterized by degeneration of striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), yet the human-specific regulatory mechanisms that contribute to neuronal vulnerability remain poorly understood. Here, we identify HD-LINC (LINC01139), a human-specific long intergenic noncoding RNA selectively induced in symptomatic HD patient-derived MSNs (HD-MSNs) and human HD caudate. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis in HD-MSNs revealed that HD-LINC was enriched in a symptomatic HD neuronal state associated with lipid metabolic and protein clearance regulation, while not observed in non-degenerative reprogrammed MSNs derived from pre-manifest HD individuals. Reducing HD-LINC attenuated mutant HTT aggregation, dystrophic neurites, DNA damage, and neuronal death, whereas HD-LINC overexpression exacerbated these phenotypes. Transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses further implicated HD-LINC in neuronal lipid regulation. We found that HD-MSNs exhibited aberrant accumulation of enlarged, low-mobility lipid droplets (LDs) within neurites, a previously unrecognized phenotype in patient-derived neurons. Critically, increased lipid peroxidation was observed within LD-enriched dystrophic neurites in HD-MSNs. HD-LINC knockdown cleared neuritic LD accumulation, restored soma-enriched LD distribution, and reduced lipid peroxidation. Finally, we developed antisense oligonucleotides that effectively reduced HD-LINC and reversed HD-LINC-associated phenotypes, nominating HD-LINC lowering as a potential therapeutic strategy in HD. These results identify HD-LINC as a human-specific regulator of neuronal LD spatial organization, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal degeneration in HD. They further reveal dysregulated neuritic LD accumulation driven by HD-LINC, and highlight lincRNA-mediated lipid dysregulation as a significant contributor to neuronal vulnerability to degeneration.

abstract: Over the past decade, CRISPR-Cas based biosensors have emerged as sensitive, specific and programmable platforms for nucleic acid detection, with applications ranging from diagnostic tools, environmental monitoring and various applications in fundamental research. The vast majority of these biosensors are currently limited to in vitro applications, highlighting the need for cellular platforms. Here, we provide a perspective on the potential of type III CRISPR-Cas systems as a platform for real-time RNA biosensing in living cells. We discuss the unique properties that distinguish type III from other CRISPR-Cas types, including their intrinsic cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signal amplification cascade, PAM-free RNA targeting and the extensive biochemical diversity of their downstream CARF and SAVED effector proteins. We outline the fundamental design principles of a genetically encoded type III cellular biosensor, comprising a programmable guide RNA, a multi-subunit sensing complex and a cOA-sensing effector protein capable of generating optical or electrochemical readout signals. A remaining challenge for type III cellular biosensors is the inherent cytotoxicity of canonical cOA-activated effectors. We propose several strategies to re-engineer these outputs towards non-cytotoxic reporter systems. While cellular biosensors present a natural route toward in vivo sensing, they face many challenges beyond the choice of the output signal and hardware strategy. We conclude that type III CRISPR-Cas is a promising platform for programmable real-time RNA sensing in living cells, utilizing its diverse modular effector outputs, representing a significant expansion of the CRISPR biosensor toolkit, while emphasizing appropriate deployment scenarios that enables full potential of these biosensors.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the management of mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the ~95% of patients with mismatch repair-proficient/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) disease derive little benefit owing to an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME), poor T-cell infiltration, myeloid dominance, TGF-β-enriched stroma, and the systemically immunosuppressive milieu imposed by hepatic metastases. Clinically tested combinations-multikinase inhibitor plus anti-PD-1, Fc-enhanced dual checkpoint blockade, chemotherapy- or antiangiogenic-ICI regimens-have so far produced modest, largely non-durable response rates that are further attenuated in liver-metastatic disease, motivating approaches that pharmacologically remodel the TME rather than only release checkpoint restraint.
OBJECTIVE: To provide an evidence-stratified synthesis of nanotechnology-enabled immunotherapy in CRC that explicitly separates (a) clinically established evidence, (b) strategies under early-phase clinical investigation, and (c) concepts that remain preclinical or are extrapolated from other tumor types, and to derive from this appraisal a biomarker-enriched translational research agenda.
METHODS: Narrative, integrative (non-systematic) review. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ASCO/ESMO/AACR proceedings were searched from January 2010 through April 2026. Each strategy was appraised according to the highest available level of evidence, the tumor type and model system in which the evidence was generated, and its demonstrated CRC specificity.
RESULTS: In current clinical practice, nanomedicine in CRC is essentially limited to nanoparticle-formulated cytotoxics exploited for pharmacokinetic advantage (e.g. liposomal irinotecan), whereas nano-enabled immunotherapy is confined to a small number of early-phase trials-most notably lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccines in ctDNA-positive resected CRC and hafnium-oxide nanoparticle radioenhancers-none of which has yet demonstrated a progression-free or overall survival benefit in MSS CRC. Against this background we critically appraise six classes of strategy: (i) LNP-based mRNA neoantigen vaccines; (ii) polymeric and inorganic nanocarriers for STING and TLR agonists; (iii) tumor-associated macrophage-repolarizing nanoparticles; (iv) nano-radiosensitizers and photothermal/photodynamic platforms priming immunogenic cell death; (v) nano-formulated checkpoint inhibitor delivery; and (vi) locoregional nano-strategies directed at hepatic metastasis-specific immunosuppression. For categories (ii)-(vi) the supporting evidence is predominantly murine (largely subcutaneous CT26/MC38 models) or extrapolated from immunologically "hot" tumors such as melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer, in which both the underlying biology and the checkpoint backbone differ materially from MSS CRC. Recurrent translational barriers include low, highly heterogeneous nanoparticle accumulation in human tumors, dense TGF-β-rich stroma and elevated interstitial pressure, mononuclear phagocyte system clearance, liver-metastasis-specific tolerance that subcutaneous models do not reproduce, unresolved manufacturing/CMC and regulatory pathways, and the absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers of intratumoral immune conversion.
CONCLUSION: Nanotechnology offers a mechanistically coherent and experimentally testable-but at present clinically unproven-set of strategies for converting "cold" MSS CRC into immune-responsive disease. We therefore position nano-enabled immunotherapy as a research priority rather than an imminent standard of care, and argue that its clinical value can only be established through biomarker-enriched, paired-biopsy early-phase trials with pharmacodynamic endpoints of immune conversion and prospective stratification by metastatic site (particularly hepatic involvement) and consensus molecular subtype.
LIMITATIONS: This is a narrative rather than systematic review; it is therefore subject to selection and publication bias, and much of the evidence synthesized is preclinical and of limited direct translational certainty.

abstract: Rapid and accurate diagnostics are essential for controlling emerging infectious diseases and antimicrobial resistance, yet CRISPR assays with exceptional analytical sensitivity often remain difficult to translate into deployable tests. Existing reviews have commonly organized CRISPR diagnostics by Cas effector, biosensor format, or application, offering limited guidance on how design decisions interact across complete workflows or why promising systems remain at the proof-of-concept stage. We introduce an integrated framework that connects five coupled design layers with five levels of translational evidence. The design layers comprise guide RNA engineering, signal amplification circuits, molecular adaptors, computational design support, and specimen and intended-use implementation. The evidence levels progress from purified-target characterization and spiked-matrix testing to retrospective specimen evaluation, prospective integrated-workflow evaluation, and intended-use operation by target users supported by controls, usability assessment, real-time stability, manufacturing consistency, cost per valid result, and claim-specific regulatory preparation. This dual framework shows how improvements at one layer can shift the dominant bottleneck to another. For example, preamplification can lower the analytical limit of detection while increasing contamination risk and workflow burden, whereas guide designs that improve sequence discrimination may reduce cognate-target activation. The framework supports bottleneck-guided selection of effectors, signal-gain strategies, adaptors, computational tools, and multiplexing formats according to target type and abundance, specimen matrix, intended decision, target users, and deployment setting. High analytical sensitivity or single-nucleotide discrimination under controlled conditions does not establish clinical utility unless such performance improves classification at the intended decision threshold within the complete workflow. Translation requires standardized benchmarking, matrix-aware validation, appropriate controls, stability and manufacturability assessment, prospective intended-use studies, and economic evaluation suited to the intended claim and setting. This framework shifts the evaluation of CRISPR diagnostics from isolated analytical performance toward evidence-based workflow co-design.
